posts.title: AI Runs on Our Water, Our Power and Our Work. What Should We Get Back?
posts.subtitle: What Alaska's oil dividend can teach California about claiming our share of AI
posts.author: mBOLDen Change and Minh Ngo
posts.excerpt: What Alaska's oil dividend can teach California about claiming our share of AI
posts.html:
Voters in California recently rejected the “billionaire tax” and passed Prop. 42, constitutionally banning new wealth taxes. This outcome will almost certainly spend the next few years being litigated before landing back on a future ballot — this is CA after all and we apparently enjoy doing things twice.

But for today, let’s step around that particular fight (and the current soap opera at the top of Nvidia, a reminder of how much of this economy rides on a handful of people) and ask this basic question: since AI extracts our water, our power and our work product, what should we get back?

Saying the Quiet Part Out Loud

Usually, conversations about whether the public deserves a cut of an industry’s profits leads to accusations of wanting to stifle innovation or a lecture on the pitfalls of communism. But the tech giants building these systems aren’t talking about AI like it’s a better product or stepped-up innovation. They talk about it like it’s the asteroid that took out the dinosaurs.

Sam Altman and Dario Amodei have openly floated the idea of using AI’s massive profits to offset the economic upheaval their own technology might cause. This spring, OpenAI even published a paper calling for a public wealth fund, also writing:

“AI data centers should pay their own way on energy so that households aren’t subsidizing them.” - OpenAI, Industrial Policy for the Intelligence Age: Ideas to Keep People First

And in May 2026, Governor Newsom ordered state agencies to study revenue-sharing models alongside severance standards and retraining.

So the debate isn’t whether the public should share in the wealth AI creates or protected from the upheaval that is to come. Many of the evangelists behind the AI boom have already conceded this point. The question then is why we’re owed a share. Whether we frame this as “corporate charity,” a “safety net for displaced humans” or “royalties for using our shared resources” changes what comes next.

Every AI Model Is Built on Something We Already Paid For

AI models were trained on generations of human work product across literature, art, math, science, engineering, philosophy and much more that has been lifted off of the internet. Of course, the internet itself started as a publicly funded government project, with public universities training many of the researchers building these systems. At the end of the day, the companies behind these AI models have never received an invoice requiring them to pay for this knowledge.

And then there’s the physical infrastructure. AI is run through giant, windowless warehouses that guzzle absurd amounts of water and electricity. In California, that comes straight out of natural resources and shared systems we all subsidize. Between 2019 and 2023, electricity use by California data centers nearly doubled, from 5.54 to 10.82 terawatt-hours, and their water use nearly doubled right alongside it. We’re talking about the same water Central Valley farmers ration during a drought, and the same electrical grid households pay for every month to keep their AC or heat on.

What Alaska Figured Out 50 Years Ago

Who owns Alaska’s oil? The answer is found in their state constitution: Alaska’s natural resources belong to the state, held for the maximum benefit of its people.

In 1976, voters created the Permanent Fund, which captures at least 25% of the state’s mineral royalties. And since 1982, it has produced an annual dividend check to nearly every resident, more than 600,000 people a year.

Because of how it was set up, Alaskans don’t treat that check like government welfare. It’s simply the people’s cut of a resource that exists for the common good. Economists have also studied the fund for decades and found it didn’t push people out of work, which is one of the most trotted-out talking points against giving people cash.

What We Can Adapt from Alaska

Alaska provides a possible pathway forward. It also shows us the potholes and gaps on the path that we should avoid.

  • The potholes. Since 2018, Alaska has pulled about 5% of the fund’s value each year, with lawmakers deciding how to split it between residents and the state budget. In 2025, the legislature used 85% of the money drawn from the fund that year to cover government spending, shrinking the dividend to $1,000, the lowest in state history after inflation. With no state income tax, the fund now pays for over half of state operations. The lesson is that if we are able to build a fund, we also need to protect the payout from being directed to supplement the state’s general fund.

  • This does not replace a real safety net. In recent years, Alaska’s payouts usually landed between $1,000 and $2,000. That’s great for winter heating bills or back-to-school shoes and clothing. It won’t save families from falling over the cliff if their jobs and careers are all but eliminated. If AI disrupts the job market the way its creators claim it will, we need to reimagine what economic security and a sustainable safety net looks like for everyone.

  • Oil is anchored. AI tech is not. Alaska could collect royalties on the oil because it was physically anchored to the land. And yes, AI companies could move out of the state to avoid some taxes or regulation. But while you can move a company’s headquarters to Texas in an afternoon, you cannot move the Central Valley’s water, California’s power lines, the existing data centers or the millions of Californians feeding these models every day. To have a public claim that actually sticks, we need to anchor it to the resources that can’t leave.

So, What’s the Solution?

If AI runs on public water, public power and our collective brainpower, what’s a fair cut for the public? And how do we build something permanent instead of a pilot that ends when the grant does (a cycle mBOLDen Change and every other nonprofit knows firsthand)?

I don’t have a pretty bow to tie all of this together. I do think viewing AI as resource extraction of public resources opens doors to a different conversation that isn’t about wealth taxes.

There is also a movement picking up steam about a "national AI dividend." But until states like California take the lead, a national dividend feels more like a nice panel discussion than a reality.

posts.title: It's DAF Day: Who Decides Where Your Money Goes?
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: Today is DAF Day, a national day of giving for donor-advised funds (3.5 million+ accounts holding more than $326 billion in charitable assets).
posts.html:
Today is DAF Day, a national day of giving for donor-advised funds (3.5 million+ accounts holding more than $326 billion in charitable assets).

Did you know that once your money is in a DAF, the sponsor has the final say over where it goes and not you? So if you have a DAF, today is a good day to look at where your charitable assets sit.

In May we wrote about how Fidelity Charitable, Vanguard Charitable, DAFgiving360 and Goldman Sachs Philanthropy Fund froze grants to the Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) because of a politically motivated indictment. Fidelity and Vanguard called the freeze temporary while the case moved forward.

The trial had been set for this month, but it has now been pushed into 2027. This means that the funding freeze will have been in effect for over a full year before a trier of fact or law weighs in.

Today, the SPLC remains a 501(c)(3) in good standing. But that hasn’t stopped the chill from spreading. Benevity, the platform behind many corporate employee giving programs, has deactivated the SPLC’s profile. As ProPublica reported, the SPLC still hasn’t been told why it was cut off or whether there is any path to reinstatement.

As we said then: “you don’t have to indict a thousand organizations to silence a movement.”

In honor of DAF Day, we updated our Move My DAF scorecard today.

See where your DAF sponsor stands

If your DAF is with one that froze funding, you can move it. It takes four to eight weeks, has no tax consequences and requires no reason.

posts.title: Tying It All Together
posts.subtitle: Reflections on the festival of Raksha Bandhan and caring for those we love
posts.author: mBOLDen Change and Rishi Narain
posts.excerpt: Reflections on the festival of Raksha Bandhan and caring for those we love
posts.html:
This is a guest piece written by former staff member and longtime volunteer Rishi Narain. Rishi’s reflection takes our usual conversations about social infrastructure and brings them home: looking at family, the cost of protection, and what we owe to one another.

The views here are the author’s own.

Raksha Bandhan fell on August 28th this year, a wonderful festival observed by many in India. It’s one of my favorites, and not just because it involves the giving of sweets. After all, most festivals in India do.

During this festival, brothers pledged protection to their sisters, who would symbolically tie Rakhi on their brother’s wrist as a reminder of that promise, and pray for their safety and prosperity. And in true Indian fashion, they fed their brother sweets, because we all know the way to an Indian man’s heart is through his stomach. Which is, I suppose, to say that we should be judged by the way we treat the women who feed us.

So as my sister and I sat down as we have for every year of my life, I happily ate Greek Baklava (very traditional) and reflected on what it meant to pledge protection to my sister. And to understand that, I should tell you about her.

She’s almost 10 years older than me, which means she had a hand in raising me. She loves Bollywood movies and music, especially the disco inspired sounds of the 70s. Let’s just say I don’t share her tastes. She’s something of a Disney adult. I’d make fun of her, but my ideal birthday is being left alone to marathon the Lord of the Rings trilogy, so maybe I shouldn’t throw stones, as the good book teaches. She’s been at this grown up thing longer than me, and I think she might be better at it than I am. She runs a successful Coaching and Communications business and has spent most of her life speaking in front of groups, which was always a challenge for me.

There’s one thing I haven’t explained about her, and it’s always a bit tricky for me. Because people should be allowed to define themselves.

My sister is legally blind.

I say this is tricky to explain because if I say she is legally blind, you might think that’s the most important thing about her. And admittedly, when we have to go somewhere she’s never been or do something she’s never done, it is the most important thing.

And I find that explaining it has her having a disability may not be the right way to go about it.

It might be more accurate to say she is Political.

And I don’t just mean that she likes to talk politics (we both do and do so frequently).

What I mean is that her existence is something that gets voted on by society. These things happen when you are disabled, a woman, a minority, an immigrant.

So, when I have to think about her protection, it becomes readily apparent that I alone can’t provide that. If I just had a sister who loved Disney, 70s Bollywood and a bottle of Coke and has religiously watched Young and the Restless since before I was born, it would be token protection.

But alas, it’s not that simple.

But alas, it’s not that simple.

My sister was not born blind. When she was 10, she had a near fatal reaction to a medication that left her with burns over 2/3rds of her body and destroyed her body’s natural ability to produce tears. The reaction also resulted in her having severe underlying respiratory issues.

Which is all to say that the COVID 19 pandemic was our personal hell.

Our family watched the news more closely than most, trying to make sense of a changing situation and the prospect of a disease that attacked the vulnerable and killed them by suffocating them.

I know some people claimed that being forced to take a vaccine was somehow against their religion.

And I will admit to thinking some downright sinful things about them, because my sister basically couldn’t leave the house for the better part of 4 years because people wanted the freedom to go out. And I’m a bit upset by that because my family wanted the same thing. It doesn’t quite feel fair that there’s a price for that kind of thing when you have to pay it.

I don’t really ask people for their opinion on COVID anymore. It’s fairly straightforward to me. Take the vaccine or else just admit that you think my sister should just stay home, and if she dies, she dies. And I’m not afraid to put it in terms that blunt.

Needless to say, I don’t get a lot of feedback after that.

So, I do find myself asking the question of what it takes to protect my sister. And the fact is, it’s very simple. It takes money to protect her.

I do think a lot about my late father, who was told he could probably sue the doctor who prescribed her the medicine over the phone from a golf course -- and receive a lot of money. His response was that he didn’t need anyone else’s money, he could take care of his own daughter. My dad was a proud man who had a strong sense of honor. I’d like to think I learned some of that from him.

I think about how he was able to keep a roof over our heads, pay for my sister’s care, find money to send my sister, and later me, to college (though in my case it was posthumously), and take us on the occasional vacation, all while earning 90% of our family’s income. I’m like a lot of men my age. We have an example from our fathers who made life look easy in a different day in age.

I earn more money than my dad ever did, but it feels like I can barely keep up taking care of myself.

Which is to say, I need help. And so do many others who have family members with needs. And it seems as though every day, another agency which used to provide support to vulnerable people has no money to spend, while at the same time the National Debt climbs to record highs, and we fight a meaningless war in the Middle East. We have always been at war in the Middle East. And there is no money to spend.

Governments at all levels are increasing surveillance of the people. When your sister is blind, you take a dim view of surveillance, because the phrase “it won’t affect you if you have nothing to hide” sounds even more like a threat. Anyone who makes that argument doesn’t have to worry about protecting someone who may be unable to protect themselves. And if we lose that, I wonder if we have anything worth keeping at all. It’s hard to put a price on something like that.

So, this year I find I must do that thing that I loathe most, which is ask for help when it comes to caring for my family. I am honor bound to protect her because she is my sister, and I am a dutiful Indian man. We care a great deal about our own honor. And sometimes we must accept that others come first. It’s a lesson I’ve had a hard time learning. I may need some help with that.

So maybe it’s a good thing that I am also American man. In both nations, it should be our privilege to care for one another.

I hope that with the many ways the world is changing, our commitment to protect those who need help has not been lost. The way I see it, I think we have the money, it’s a matter of how we spend it.

I want to protect my sister. And I want to protect everyone who isn’t my sister. I think the way we do that is to live in a peaceful world.

I may be biased, but I think the world is a better place with my sister in it. But it is also my duty to extend that same sentiment to those who may not have a brother they tie Rakhi on.

I hope our compassion is not bound simply with thread.

posts.title: Citizenship: "The Right to Have Rights"
posts.subtitle: The Supreme Court just upheld birthright citizenship. In our 250th year, it's worth remembering what that promise is for.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: The Supreme Court just upheld birthright citizenship. In our 250th year, it's worth remembering what that promise is for.
posts.html:
“Citizenship is the right to have rights... The Framers of the Fourteenth Amendment extended that promise to ‘every free-born person in this land.’ We keep that promise today.” — Chief Justice John Roberts

Today, the U.S. Supreme Court delivered a monumental ruling, striking down the administration’s executive order and resoundingly upholding the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship. By reaffirming that anyone born on American soil is a citizen, the Court protected a foundational pillar of American democracy.

Rooted in 250 Years of the American Promise

As our nation marks its semiquincentennial, 250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence, this ruling is a reminder of what America is supposed to stand for. For two and a half centuries, the American experiment has wrestled with the ideals of equality, freedom, and inclusion.

Birthright citizenship is no cure for inequality. A hereditary underclass still exists in many forms across this country. But it provides the legal bedrock that prevents permanent, institutionalized exclusion from our democracy. Without it, the rights required to fight for true equality wouldn’t even be on the table.

It ensures the promise of America can still belong to the next generation, no matter where their parents came from. Today, SCOTUS made clear that a president cannot rewrite the Constitution by executive fiat.

The Work Ahead

The political and legislative battles will continue.

A single court victory secures the baseline. It does not halt the apparatus seeking to restrict who gets to be considered “American.” Courts interpret the Constitution; they do not write law. The same effort that reached the Court by executive order can return through legislation, funding fights, and quieter policy maneuvers built to erode the rights of immigrant communities.

The legal question is settled for now. Keeping our elected leaders accountable is the ongoing work, and it belongs to all of us.

As we mark our nation’s 250th anniversary, we can be relieved that a foundational constitutional right withstood this latest assault.

Except for the Indigenous peoples who were here first, every American is an immigrant or the descendant of someone who crossed an ocean or a border to build a life here. That is the true fabric of this nation.

Let’s carry that conviction forward.

posts.title: The Invisible Guillotine
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: In 1981, a nineteen-year-old named Michael Donald was lynched by the KKK in Mobile, Alabama.
posts.html:
In 1981, a nineteen-year-old named Michael Donald was lynched by the KKK in Mobile, Alabama. He was chosen at random. The killers wanted to send a message.

The Southern Poverty Law Center sent one back. In 1987, they won a $7 million judgment against the United Klans of America. The Klan couldn’t pay, so they surrendered their national headquarters. That building was the spine of white supremacy in America. The SPLC broke it.

For fifty years, that has been the work: doing what bigger, “safer” institutions were often too cautious to do. Naming hate. Suing it. Dismantling it.

Then came April 2026.

The Justice Department indicted the SPLC on federal charges. Before a single court weighed the facts, four of the largest financial companies in America cut them off.

Fidelity Charitable. Vanguard Charitable. DAFgiving360 (Schwab). Goldman Sachs Philanthropy Fund.

These companies manage hundreds of billions in donor-advised funds — accounts where donors deposit money for charitable giving, take the tax deduction upfront, and direct grants to organizations over time. When the indictment dropped, they froze the SPLC’s access: before a trial, a verdict, or a shred of proven wrongdoing. Without due process.

The indictment is paper thin and widely condemned as politically motivated. Former federal prosecutors and legal scholars say it is unlikely to survive a courtroom.

The Myth of Neutrality

These institutions will tell you they are just following blanket policies. They call it being “neutral.”

There is no such thing as a neutral freeze.

When you cut off a civil rights organization based solely on a government charge — one that hasn’t been tested in court — you aren’t staying out of the fight. You are picking a side. You are handing the federal government a defunding mechanism that doesn’t require prevailing in court. Fred Blackwell, CEO of the San Francisco Foundation, said it plainly:

“Giving platforms are not acting neutrally when they cut off access to charitable resources based solely on a charge, before any court has weighed the facts. They are imposing a penalty in advance of due process.”

In moments like this, neutrality is just a polite word for complicity.

Not every DAF sponsor made the same call. The San Francisco Foundation, AUM+ (Assets Under Movement), Tides Foundation, ImpactAssets and others held the line — continuing to allow grants to the SPLC because it remains an IRS-recognized nonprofit in good standing.

The difference between these choices is not law or policy. It is about whose interests come first.

The Climate of Compliance

The indictment is the loud part. There is a quieter, more dangerous trend underneath it.

When President Trump signed the January 2025 executive orders banning the language of diversity and racial justice in federal contracting, it wasn’t just a policy shift. It was a signal. Many corporations, foundations and nonprofits immediately scrubbed their mission statements, replacing “racial justice” and “equity” with language designed to survive the Trump administration’s panopticon.

They don’t necessarily want to shut these organizations down. Closed organizations become martyrs. They want them to stay open, but be quiet. Alive. Funded. And no longer themselves.

The SPLC has nearly $800 million in reserves. They will outlast this. The point is you don’t have to indict a thousand organizations to silence a movement. You indict one — visibly, publicly, with a press conference — and let the rest wrestle with how much their mission is worth the risk.

For the small nonprofit fighting for voting rights in Georgia, immigrant rights in Arizona or reproductive rights in Texas, the message is already received: this is what it costs to do this work. Most can’t afford to find out if they’re next.

Make Your Move

If you have a DAF at Fidelity, Vanguard, Schwab, Goldman or any other sponsor that doesn’t reflect your values, you can move your assets to where they can do good. This is why we built Move My DAF, a guide and a directory to encourage donors to think through their values and the implications of who “manages” their DAF.

There are no tax consequences. Your history, your deductions, and your capital all transfer with you. It takes approximately four to eight weeks and some paperwork. And you are not required to give a reason.

Fidelity distributed $18.3 billion in grants last year. It and other sponsors can afford to lose donors. What they cannot afford is to lose the trust of donors who expect their charitable intent to be protected, not policed. Every account that moves makes that argument loudly and in the only language these institutions understand and value.

And for mBOLDen Change, this is the first step in a larger push to ensure that the hundreds of billions of dollars set aside for community impact are managed by institutions that actually prioritize the public good.

posts.title: Forty Years of the Same Con
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: Four decades of trickle-down economics has worked out great.
posts.html:
Four decades of trickle-down economics has worked out great. For the wealthy.

For the three decades before 1980, American incomes at the top and the bottom of the ladder rose at roughly the same pace. If inequality hadn’t dramatically widened starting in 1980, how much would the average working family be earning in 2026? Around $145,000. Instead, the median household earns $80,000.

What changed? From 1936 to 1980, the top income tax rate for individuals was 70% or higher. Today it’s 37%. During this same time, the social safety net has been gutted to pay for tax cuts that benefit the wealthiest households.

Reaganomics: Reverse Robinhood as Policy

In 1981, President Ronald Reagan signed a 185-page bill called the Economic Recovery Tax Act on his 688-acre ranch above Santa Barbara. His bill cut the top income tax rate from 70% to 50%. It carved a $750 billion hole in the federal budget. And Reagan delivered the pitch that would be repeated, in almost the same words, for the next forty years: cut taxes at the top, and the rewards will reach everyone.

In 1986, Reagan doubled down and boldly declared that his 1986 Tax Reform Act “is perhaps the greatest antipoverty program in history. It will take 6 million poor people off the income tax rolls entirely.” The receipts said otherwise.

The next administration ran the same play.

George W. Bush’s 2001 and 2003 cuts handed the top 1% of households an average tax break of $570,000 over the eight years that followed. A new category called “qualified dividends” was invented to let wealthy investors pay 15% on their dividend income instead of 35%. The nurses and teachers whose retirement accounts held a few mutual funds might have saved a couple hundred dollars from that change. The hedge-fund managers and corporate executives whose wealth sat in dividend-paying equities saved tens of thousands.

Then came Donald Trump. His administration’s 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act delivered tax cuts of roughly $61,500 to households in the top 1%, and about $100 to households in the bottom 20%. One household got a down payment on a second home. The other got a tank of gas. In 2025, Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill doubled down on poverty with low-income children among the hardest hit.

And he’s not done yet. In early April, the White House submitted a FY2027 budget that would cut domestic spending to its lowest levels since Eisenhower  while boosting military spending to $1.5 trillion.

Today, the tax code is critical infrastructure for the ultra wealthy. It has been leveraged by every Republican administration since Reagan to expand wealth and opportunity for the few. The tax cuts and infrastructure have remained mostly untouched under every Democrat who followed.

View this on Substack

And it is not just federal. The same values have been metabolized in statehouses across the country.

What You Can Do This Tax Week

The tax code hard-codes unfairness for tens of millions of American families. This Tax Week, join us in demanding one that works for all of us.

  • Contact your senators and representative. Tell them working families need a tax code that is critical infrastructure for workers, not the wealthy. The One Big Beautiful Bill cut $1 trillion from Medicaid and handed $1 trillion in tax giveaways to the top 1%. Trump’s FY2027 budget proposes to cut even deeper.

  • Check your statehouse calendar. Progressive tax measures — from billionaire taxes in California to wealth tax proposals in statehouses across the country — are being debated right now. So are copycat measures that mirror OBBBA’s Medicaid work requirements and documentation barriers. State legislative calendars are public. Know what yours is considering.

Forty years of the same con is not a policy failure. The tax code is working as intended  —  just not for most of us. Use your voice. If you need inspiration, our friends at Americans for Tax Fairness put together a toolkit to make it easy.

posts.title: The "Cover Charge" for Democracy
posts.subtitle: The SAVE Act Isn't Just About Voting. It's About Who Gets to Participate in America.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: The SAVE Act Isn't Just About Voting. It's About Who Gets to Participate in America.
posts.html:
The U.S. Senate is expected to vote on the SAVE America Act this week. If you’ve followed the coverage, you’ve heard the headline version: a bill requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote, passed by the House in February at President Trump’s urging.

Most of the opposition has rightly focused on what this bill would do to elections. We agree. The SAVE Act is a solution without a problem. Utah reviewed its entire voter roll of more than two million registrations and found exactly one confirmed case of noncitizen registration and zero instances of noncitizen voting.

But we want to broaden the frame. The SAVE Act is a systemic barrier dressed up as election security.

From Systems of Trust to Systems of Suspicion

At mBOLDen Change, we are on the ground and in the community every day, responding to the immediate needs of families facing economic instability and the aftermath of disasters. But we also know that direct service isn’t enough. We work upstream because you cannot create lasting change without fixing the systems that create the crises in the first place.

And here is what working upstream has taught us: when you design a system — whether it’s for healthcare, disaster relief, housing, or elections — you face a fundamental choice. You can design for the 99 percent of people who are acting in good faith. Or you can design a high-suspicion system that treats every neighbor as a potential fraud.

Since 1993, the National Voter Registration Act has relied on a system of attestation under penalty of perjury. You sign a form swearing you are a citizen, knowing that a false statement carries up to five years in federal prison, deportation, and permanent revocation of legal status. It works. The SAVE Act replaces this system of trust with a high-suspicion gauntlet. It assumes that unless you can produce a $165 passport, your voice doesn’t belong in the conversation. And it weaponizes the same paperwork trap that we see keeping people locked out of the economy every single day.

The “Document Trap”

The bill requires “documentary proof of citizenship” — usually a passport or an original birth certificate — to be presented in person. According to the Brennan Center, 21.3 million eligible American citizens do not have these documents readily available.

For many people, “documentary proof” sounds like a simple chore. Dig through a filing cabinet, find the certificate, done.

But for a senior born at home in a rural area decades ago, there may be no birth certificate to find. For a survivor of a house fire or wildfire, that piece of paper burned along with everything else. For a young person aging out of foster care, documents were lost somewhere between placements.

For many, it is not just a matter of finding a folder. It is a matter of legal identity. An estimated 69 million married women have a current legal name that does not match their birth certificate. For a trans American who has updated their legal identity, the same problem applies. Under the SAVE Act, a standard REAL ID is insufficient because it only confirms “lawful presence,” not citizenship status — and only six states even offer a version that indicates citizenship. For naturalized Americans, the scrutiny is compounded by intimidation: the SAVE Act would force them to dig up specialized federal papers they may not have needed for years, effectively treating their citizenship as a provisional status that must be re-proven at every turn.

These aren’t edge cases. They are millions of people.

When we make a birth certificate the cover charge for democracy, we are not securing an election. We are taxing the most vulnerable among us for the right to be heard. And the people who cannot easily produce a passport or birth certificate are not randomly distributed across the population. They are disproportionately low-income, disproportionately people of color, disproportionately rural, disproportionately the same families and communities we work alongside every day — people already navigating systems designed to make stability hard to reach.

This is the point the election-security frame misses. The SAVE Act does not create a new barrier. It extends an existing one — the same documentation gauntlet that already excludes millions from banking, housing, employment, and public benefits — to the one mechanism those communities have to change the system: their vote.

A Recipe for Systemic Collapse

This isn’t just bad policy. It is a recipe for chaos.

The SAVE Act contains no transition period and no funding for implementation. If passed, it would break the voter registration process overnight, leaving local election officials — your neighbors who run the polls — holding the bag with no resources, no guidance, and no time.

The bill would end online voter registration in the 43 states and D.C. that currently offer it. It would eliminate registration by mail. It would shut down voter registration drives nationwide. And it would take effect immediately.

We have seen this play out before. Kansas imposed a proof-of-citizenship requirement over a decade ago and ended up blocking 31,000 eligible U.S. citizens from registering — 12 percent of all first-time applicants — before the courts stepped in. Now, states like Florida have already passed their own versions.

It gets worse. The bill authorizes private individuals to sue election officials directly if they believe a voter was registered without the proper paperwork. This is not government oversight. It is a green light for vigilante litigation against the neighbors who run our polls. A civic duty becomes a legal minefield, where a simple clerical error could trigger a lawsuit.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration’s own Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity was disbanded because it could not find evidence of the widespread fraud this bill claims to address. States already verify citizenship through Social Security numbers and driver’s license data. Election officials already use federal databases to confirm eligibility. The existing system works. The SAVE Act would dismantle it in the name of solving a problem that doesn’t exist.

The Federal Fight Is the Headline. The Systemic Exclusion Is Being Built in Statehouses.

Forty-three states have introduced or are considering copycat proof-of-citizenship legislation. This is not a single bill. It is a coordinated effort to narrow who counts as a full participant in American civic life — and it will not stop at the federal level.

The communities that would lose their ability to register under these bills are the same ones fighting for the policies that would actually address poverty, inequality, and exclusion. That is not a coincidence. When you design a system around suspicion, the people with the least resources to navigate it are the ones who get locked out. When those same people are also the ones most affected by decisions about housing, healthcare, wages, and public investment, stripping their voice is not a procedural inconvenience. It is a political strategy.

What You Can Do — This Week

The Senate vote is imminent. This is a moment where individual action matters.

  • Call your Senators. Tell them you are calling to ask them to protect the systemic health of our democracy by opposing the SAVE Act’s administrative burdens on eligible voters. You can find your Senators and their phone numbers at senate.gov.

  • Check your state. The federal fight is the headline, but the systemic exclusion is being built in statehouses across the country. Check your local legislative calendar for proof-of-citizenship bills. The Voting Rights Lab tracks state-level legislation.

  • Share this piece. The election-security frame dominates the conversation. Help broaden it. The people who would lose their right to vote under the SAVE Act are the same people already fighting to participate in an economy and a democracy that weren’t built for them.

At mBOLDen Change, we believe that systems change requires changing who has power in those systems. The SAVE Act is designed to make sure that doesn’t happen. It is built on suspicion, enforced through paperwork, and aimed at the people with the least margin to fight back. The American people should reject it.

posts.title: Stop Bringing Spreadsheets to a Values Fight
posts.subtitle: What lies beneath every policy — and why it's the case we need to be making.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: What lies beneath every policy — and why it's the case we need to be making.
posts.html:
At mBOLDen Change, values aren’t what we say or believe. They are what we do. They are the sum total of our collective choices. They show up in what we build, who we center, and what we are willing to name out loud.

This shapes how we work. It also shapes the question we keep coming back to: What do our choices — as an organization, as communities, as individuals — reveal about what we deeply value?

We cannot build a world rooted in dignity by treating policies and structures as piecemeal problems. The work starts deeper — with the values underneath, the ones embedded in the systems we’ve inherited and the ones we’re choosing to keep. Before we can change the rules, we have to be honest about what the current rules actually say about us.

Holding Up the Mirror

We often treat the economy like the weather — something that happens to us, unpredictable and out of our control. But the affordability crisis crushing American families isn’t an act of fate. It is a policy and market design.

When gas prices surge while corporate margins reach historic highs, that isn’t a glitch. When a nurse in rural community watches her hospital close because someone decided her patients weren’t profitable enough to save, that isn’t a math problem. When a family pays $27,000 a year for health insurance and still can’t afford their daughter’s insulin, that isn’t bad luck. These are moral choices — made by specific people, protected by specific systems.

If you want to know what a society truly values, don’t look at its slogans.

Look at its safety net: who we catch and who we’ve decided is expendable. Look at its economic rules: who they were written to empower and who they were designed to leave behind. Look at the receipt — the impact tally of our collective priorities, where a trillion dollars in healthcare cuts and a 400% increase in the ICE budget sit on the same ledger as permanent tax cuts for the wealthiest bracket.

Our systems are a mirror. And right now, the reflection shows a preference for consolidated power over common good, and for the comfort of the few over the survival of the many.

Beyond the Spreadsheet

For too long, the conversation about our future has been reduced to mechanics — the size of a budget, the wording of a bill, the scoring of a policy. We have brought spreadsheets to a values fight.

We are arguing about percentages, when we should be arguing for humanity. The question has never been whether the wealthiest nation in history can “afford” to ensure its people can eat, heal, and learn. We can afford whatever we decide matters. The question is why we’ve been convinced that we can’t.

We are told that struggle is a natural condition of the free market economy, that scarcity is inevitable, that some must fall so others can climb. These aren’t economic laws. They are choices — choices about who deserves security and who deserves to scramble. About whose children get a foundation and whose get a lottery ticket.

And because they are choices, we can choose differently.

Making the Invisible Visible

We believe change starts by naming what we’ve been trained to accept as normal. We cannot change what we refuse to see.

This is why we launched mBOLDen Action — a project dedicated to shining a light on the systemic forces that shape daily life. We are starting with the affordability crisis because it is the most immediate receipt of how our current values are failing us, but the work won’t stop there.

Our first project, This Is Why We Can’t Have Nice Things, connects the dots between consolidated corporate power, the policy choices made in our halls of government, and the cost of living hitting families across every bracket. It traces everyday prices upstream to the companies and decisions driving them, tells the stories of real families navigating the tradeoffs, and puts what got funded next to what got cut — side by side, like a receipt.

We built it to strip away the sense that these crises are inevitable. Whether it is a tax bill that prioritizes the wealthy at the expense of the safety net, or a market designed to reward monopolies over people, these are not acts of fate. They are choices we can choose to unmake.

Values Are a Set of Actions

The shift we need isn’t only structural. It’s personal and communal. Deep social change starts with individual and community decisions — small ones, repeated, until they aren’t small anymore.

That shift is already happening around us. We see it when communities refuse to normalize the displacement of their neighbors. When people stop accepting the “inevitability” of their bills and start asking who set the price. When we collectively stop asking for permission to demand a system built on dignity.

The work ahead isn’t about changing a single policy or winning a single argument. It’s about reclaiming our power to decide what kind of world we want to build — and then building it, in how we work, how we show up for each other, and what we refuse to look away from.

Values aren’t a set of beliefs. They are a set of actions. We’re in that work. We’d like you to join us.

posts.title: Moving from Sympathy to Compassion
posts.subtitle: This guest piece is a personal reflection from Sue Sutherland, one of our longtime supporters.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: This guest piece is a personal reflection from Sue Sutherland, one of our longtime supporters.
posts.html:
More Than Words

I’d like you to take a moment to ponder three words: sympathy, empathy, and compassion. They represent a continuum I’ve been thinking about in the context of our federal safety net programs.

  • Sympathy: recognizing someone’s hardship and feeling sorry that they’re going through it.

  • Empathy: a bridge between thought and emotion—the ability to understand another person’s experience from the inside.

  • Compassion: what happens when empathy doesn’t stop at understanding, but creates an impulse to help reduce suffering.

For many of us, it can be hard to feel the impact of policy decisions on families experiencing poverty if we haven’t experienced poverty ourselves. We may feel sympathy for families struggling to stay stable, but still be unable to internalize what people are actually living through.

To better understand what budget cuts are doing to working families, I spent time with mBOLDen Change’s Safety Net Simulator. It let me take a seat at the kitchen table with families making impossible choices just to survive. I had to apply the cuts and make real tradeoffs.

It was eye-opening. It helped me understand the real-life impact of abstract policy —and it bridged the gap from sympathy, to empathy, to compassion.

I encourage you to try the Safety Net Simulator here. Policies that impact the safety net are much more than words. The simulator is one way to connect to what’s happening — but it isn’t the only way. I also hope you’ll seek out lived stories, listen to people navigating these tradeoffs, and keep finding ways to build understanding, empathy, and compassion.

With care,

Sue

posts.title: The Philanthropic Retreat
posts.subtitle: As authoritarianism advances, America's biggest foundations are choosing silence — and calling it strategy.
posts.author: Minh Ngo
posts.excerpt: As authoritarianism advances, America's biggest foundations are choosing silence — and calling it strategy.
posts.html:
The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative recently announced it was cutting 70 jobs — roughly 8 percent of its workforce — to refocus on AI-powered biomedical research. The press coverage has been characteristically credulous: a pivot to science, a doubling down on disease, a bold new chapter.

But this isn’t a pivot. It’s a purge.

Over the past year, CZI has systematically dismantled every part of its operation that touches the work this country needs most. It eliminated its Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Accessibility team. It scrubbed housing affordability and economic inclusion from its website. It gutted funding for criminal justice reform and immigration advocacy. It shuttered The Primary School, the tuition-free school Priscilla Chan herself co-founded in East Palo Alto, leaving parents scrambling. And it informed community partners across San Mateo County — many of them serving immigrant families and communities of color — that their grants would not be renewed.

CZI’s general counsel reportedly told staff the organization had become a “political target” and was “doing what we have to to avoid being sued.” A former employee put it more plainly: “They are making sure to cut anything that would sound or even be construed as DEI-esque.”

This is not a story about boldly investing in science. It is a story about cowardice dressed up as innovation.

The Pattern

The CZI layoffs are not separate from Meta’s corporate strategy. They are its philanthropic extension. And the Zuckerbergs are not alone. Across Silicon Valley and beyond, as the titans of industry have repositioned themselves to curry favor with the Trump administration, their philanthropic priorities and messaging have shifted to match. The rebranding is already underway. CZI was founded with the stated mission of building “a more inclusive, just, and healthy future for everyone.” That language has been removed from its website.

Across the philanthropic landscape, too many of the largest foundations and wealthiest individuals in the country are responding to the current political crisis with a posture that should alarm anyone who cares about what’s at stake. They are going quiet. They are rebranding equity work under palatable new names or shelving it entirely. They are protecting their assets and their access.

Wealth Warehousing

The structural incentives of American philanthropy make this retreat almost inevitable — because the structure was never really designed to move money to the people who need it. It was designed to shelter wealth and purchase social capital, while claiming the language of public good. Private foundations are required by law to distribute just 5 percent of their assets annually; even that modest threshold can be met through administrative expenses, not just grants. Private foundation assets in the United States grew twice as fast as GDP between 1985 and 2020. The Institute for Policy Studies calls them, accurately, “wealth warehousing vehicles.” That’s not a bug. That’s the product.

The largest foundations in this country increasingly operate like investment banks that happen to make grants. Their endowments grow. Their portfolios diversify. Their boards professionalize. And their actual grantmaking — the money that reaches the people and organizations doing the work — represents a shrinking fraction of their total wealth. The 5 percent floor has become a ceiling.

By Design

It is worth remembering how we got here. While there are many examples from around the world of civil society and philanthropy offering a counterweight to concentrated power, American “philanthropy” was forged by concentrated power to preserve itself. Carnegie — whose company’s private security force killed striking steelworkers at Homestead — poured his fortune into a foundation to rebuild his name. Rockefeller created his in the wake of the Standard Oil antitrust case that broke up his monopoly. In 1915, Congress convened the Walsh Commission to investigate whether these new foundations were themselves a threat to democracy — unaccountable concentrations of wealth shaping public life without public consent.

The foundations survived that scrutiny and, over time, rewrote a more flattering origin story. Some did consequential work — the Ford Foundation funded civil rights litigation when few others would. But the underlying architecture never changed: private wealth, deployed at the discretion of the wealthy, accountable to no one, and structured to grow in perpetuity.

What we are witnessing now is the architecture working as designed.

The wealthiest philanthropists in history have more resources than ever and less willingness to deploy them when it counts. They will fund what advances their business interests. What they will not fund, increasingly, is the work that puts them at odds with power.

“Thoughts and Prayers”

The inaction of major philanthropy in this moment is a form of complicity.

As the dignity, rights, and lives of people are being trampled on in our communities, the most powerful foundations in the country offer the equivalent of “thoughts and prayers.” They release carefully worded statements. They convene listening sessions. They express concern. And then they turn every community tragedy into a fundraising opportunity — for themselves. They grow their donor rolls off the crisis while the frontline organizations actually responding scramble for visibility and resources without any corresponding increase in unrestricted, long-term support.

The measure of a philanthropic institution is not its endowment or its AI strategy or its Nobel laureate advisory board. It is what it does when the question is not about left and right, but about right and wrong.

By that measure, we are witnessing a historic failure — not of resources, but of courage.

Disclosure: mBOLDen Change (formerly My New Red Shoes) has been a CZI grant recipient.

posts.title: EPA Sets the Value of Human Health at $0
posts.subtitle: How the agency’s new cost-benefit framework erases health, accountability, and environmental justice
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: How the agency’s new cost-benefit framework erases health, accountability, and environmental justice
posts.html:
The EPA’s new cost-benefit calculus tells us exactly whose lives this administration considers expendable.

For more than fifty years, the Environmental Protection Agency operated on a simple premise: protecting human health and the environment is a core responsibility of government.

That premise is now officially dead.

Under the Trump administration, the EPA has announced it will no longer factor the health benefits of reducing pollution into its cost-benefit analyses. The agency created to protect people from polluters will now calculate regulations based solely on what compliance costs industry, not on the asthma attacks prevented, the cancers avoided, or the lives saved.

This isn’t a bureaucratic tweak.

It’s a declaration of who matters, and who doesn’t.

Health No Longer Counts

For decades, the EPA relied on well-established science to quantify the benefits of reducing pollutants linked to asthma, heart disease, cancer, and premature death. Under standards finalized during the Biden administration, economists estimated that for every $1 industry invested in cutting pollution, society gained as much as $77 in health benefits. Those benefits included fewer emergency room visits, fewer missed workdays, and fewer lives cut short.

The math was straightforward. Protecting health was both morally right and economically smart.

The Trump administration looked at that equation and decided the health side no longer counted.

As The New York Times has reported, internal EPA documents show plans to repeal pollution limits on coal-fired power plants, oil refineries, steel mills, and other major industrial sources. Without counting health impact, the agency can claim that pollution regulations cost more than they’re worth.

This is not fiscal responsibility.

It is accounting fraud dressed up as policy. Human harm is erased from the ledger so the balance sheet favors polluters.

“Sacrifice Zones” by Design

An EPA spokesperson responded to criticism by insisting that “not monetizing does not equal not considering or not valuing the human health impact.”

(When a sentence is built entirely out of negations, it tells you something on its own.)

Environmental injustice has never been accidental. The communities most burdened by pollution are Black, Brown, Indigenous, low-income, and rural. They are also the communities historically excluded from political power. Highways carved through their neighborhoods. Factories sited beside their schools. Refineries built upwind of their homes.

These outcomes were not random. They were policy choices.

From the Tuskegee syphilis experiments, where Black men were deliberately denied treatment for decades, to urban renewal projects that bulldozed thriving communities of color, marginalized people have repeatedly been treated as expendable when their well-being conflicted with power’s priorities.

The EPA’s new calculus is a continuation of this history.

When regulators refuse to count the health impacts of pollution, they make a choice about whose suffering is politically acceptable. When that suffering falls overwhelmingly on communities already carrying the weight of systemic racism, the policy itself becomes the discrimination, regardless of how neutral the language sounds.

View this on Substack

The Erasure Is the Point

The Trump Administration excels at overwhelming the public with so much cruelty that no single outrage can fully register. The strategy is deliberate. If you’re busy reacting to one fire, you won’t notice three more being lit.

We understand why some people scroll past stories like this. Not out of apathy, but self-preservation. Life trains us to look away from what doesn’t immediately touch us and to assume someone else will handle it.

But environmental harm doesn’t respect zip codes forever.

The pollutants causing asthma in frontline communities travel. The water contamination poisoning a rural town doesn’t stop at property lines. The climate chaos accelerated by unchecked emissions touches everyone eventually.

Even if you believe that you could guarantee your own safety, there is still the question of what kind of society we are choosing to build.

One that weighs corporate profits against human lungs and decides the profits matter more?

One that deletes the words “Environmental Justice” from agency websites, as if erasing language could erase harm?

The erasure is the point.

If you don’t count the harm, you don’t have to answer for it.

What We Can Do

If corporate profits can be written into the equation, so can human health.

At mBOLDen Change, we believe dignity includes the right to breathe clean air and drink clean water. We refuse to normalize the unacceptable, and we will continue to name how policy choices determine who thrives and who merely survives.

Here’s how you can act:

• Contact your elected officials. Tell them you oppose any regulatory framework that excludes health impacts from cost-benefit analyses. Demand environmental justice in practice, not just rhetoric.

• Support frontline organizations collecting the data the EPA has stopped counting — like the Deep South Center for Environmental Justice, WE ACT for Environmental Justice, and California Environmental Justice Alliance.

• Stay informed and share what you learn. The Trump administration’s strategy depends on public exhaustion. Understanding what’s happening, and telling someone else, disrupts it.

Environmental justice requires more than aspiration. It requires action and policy.

posts.title: When Policy Hits the Kitchen Table
posts.subtitle: The Bill Comes Due
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: The Bill Comes Due
posts.html:
January is when many policy decisions stop being abstract and become personal.

Morgan Gunn recently learned that his health insurance would now cost him about $1,000 a month.

Just months earlier, he’d been paying what he described as a “minuscule” amount. While he was between jobs, federal tax credits kept his coverage affordable. But this December, when he left the Covered California office, the math had changed. Congress allowed those enhanced subsidies to expire in year-end budget negotiations. Mr. Gunn’s premium skyrocketed.

“I’m going to have to look at scaling back some other expenses that I don’t want to,” he told a local CBS news reporter.

This is where policy stops being a debate and becomes lived reality.

The real impact of legislation doesn’t happen at a signing ceremony or a press conference. It happens months later, when a political “win” turns into a loss on a family’s balance sheet.

View this on Substack

The Human Toll

Across California — and across the country — people are opening notices, logging into accounts, and discovering that the care they relied on now costs hundreds or thousands more each month. For some, premiums have doubled or nearly tripled. For others, coverage is simply now out of reach. Enrollment is already dropping, not because people don’t need health care, but because they can’t afford the price lawmakers have decided they should pay.

Adrienne Martin, a 47-year-old mother in Texas, is starting the year without health insurance. Her family’s monthly premium jumped from a manageable $630 to an impossible $2,400. Her husband depends on an IV medication to treat a blood-clotting disorder — medication that costs $70,000 a month without insurance.

Knowing their coverage was about to expire, the family stockpiled the drug to survive the first few months of the year.

“It would be like paying two mortgage payments. We can’t pay $30,000 a year for insurance.”

This is not a health care system. It’s financial Russian roulette with people’s lives.

This is a Feature, Not a Bug

January is when spending and budget decisions stop being abstract and become personal. Tax changes take effect. Credits expire. Policy choices made in distant chambers finally show up in household budgets. A few start the year with new advantages. Most are left to absorb the losses.

The expiration of the health care subsidies was a political choice. It reflects priorities. It reflects who mattered and who did not. And like many policy decisions, it was structured to delay accountability. The harm arrives later, after the people who made the decision have moved on — and others are left to absorb the cost.

Demand Better

If we want different outcomes in January, we have to start with different choices in November and hold leaders accountable long after the votes are counted.

Dignity should not be temporary.

And it should never be something people have to re-qualify for when the calendar turns.

This piece reflects the perspective of mBOLDen Change as we enter 2026. We believe policy should create stability, not legislate chaos into people’s lives. January doesn’t have to be a reckoning, but only if we demand better at the ballot box before the next bill comes due.

posts.title: Small Gestures
posts.subtitle: This guest piece is a personal reflection from Sue Sutherland, one of our longtime supporters.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: This guest piece is a personal reflection from Sue Sutherland, one of our longtime supporters.
posts.html:
Recently, I read an article in the Washington Post about a study on “happiness” (A 6-year research project found a surprisingly simple route to happiness by Dana Millbank). The article captured my interest by beginning with the question, “How can we stay happy in an age gone mad?”

Here’s what I learned. The six-year Cornell study found that thinking about one’s purpose and then taking a step — even a modest one — towards fulfilling it is the most efficient path to living a contented life. The study went on to say, the value is in “getting outside of yourself. Instead of focusing on the symptoms that are problematic, what if we focused on the effort and progress made toward purposeful pursuits?”

Okay. The happiness hack made sense to me. Upon reflection, my life is enriched by providing support to nonprofit organizations that closely align with my values. mBOLDen Change is one of the organizations that I support.

But then I paused . . . because framing this as a “happiness hack” made me think about who this hack is really intended to mobilize and benefit.

Marginalized communities — low-income families, immigrants, communities of color, and many others — have long shown us how purpose and connection create meaning. They live this truth every day. They show up for neighbors, share what they have, organize mutual aid, and care for one another, often under extraordinary pressure. Purpose, and the joy it can bring, isn’t absent here. It is practiced daily, even in the most challenging circumstances.

So when we talk about a “happiness hack,” I believe the invitation is really directed at people who — because of economic security, social standing, or other advantages — have the means to opt in or out of caring for others.

If you have that kind of capacity, I hope you’ll join me in committing to do more to support those navigating far greater challenges.

This holiday season, I invite you to take at least one small action that brings kindness, relief, or encouragement to someone else. A few of my favorite actions:

  • Smile and say hello to a stranger alone on the street.

  • Hold an elevator door for someone.

  • Buy a gift card for someone out in the cold.

  • Donate to a food bank.

  • Leave a larger than normal tip to a service worker.

  • Donate to a nonprofit organization whose mission resonates with you.

When we act together, small gestures can become movements.

Hope fuels action.

Action builds change.

Change renews hope.

While none of us alone can fix all the systemic forces that make the world feel overwhelming, together we can make a real difference. If we all treat purpose — and care for one another — as our own “happiness hack,” we can build a collective movement that strengthens entire communities.

Happy Holidays,

Sue Sutherland
SF Bay Area Community Volunteer

posts.title: The GoFundMe Page We Never Created
posts.subtitle: When platforms profit from generosity, trust is what gets lost.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: When platforms profit from generosity, trust is what gets lost.
posts.html:
A few weeks ago, buried in an email, was this line: “Is GoFundMe Pro competing with nonprofits?”

We followed the links, dug deeper, and discovered that GoFundMe had created a fundraising page for mBOLDen Change — without our knowledge or consent.

Our name. Our mission. Our logo. A “Donate” button.

It looked legitimate. But, it wasn’t ours.

Then we learned they’d done this to 1.4 million nonprofits across the country.

Over a million organizations — from small community groups to national charities — now have GoFundMe pages they didn’t ask for, controlled by a company that profits from those donations.

What’s Actually Happening

Here’s how it works: GoFundMe uses its search dominance to direct donors to these unauthorized pages instead of to a nonprofit’s own website. When someone donates through GoFundMe, the company takes its processing fees, encourages donors to leave “tips” for GoFundMe itself, and holds the money for up to 45 days before releasing it.

So a donation sits for weeks, then arrives with above-market fees deducted. But here’s the deeper problem: while the funds eventually reach us, we often have no way to thank the donor, share what their gift accomplished, or build a relationship.

The donation (or rather a part of it) arrives. The donor doesn’t.

That missing connection isn’t just inconvenient — it’s the difference between a transaction and a partnership. It’s how we report back on impact, invite supporters to events, share stories from the field, and ask for continued support when it matters most. Direct relationships are how nonprofits survive and grow.

By creating these pages without consent, GoFundMe inserts itself between nonprofits and their supporters: using our names and missions to drive its own revenue while severing the bonds that make organizations like ours sustainable.

This isn’t partnership.

It’s extraction.

The Bigger Picture

GoFundMe isn’t alone in using business practices that disadvantage nonprofits. Other common platforms — including Benevity and Facebook Fundraisers — present themselves as bridges between donors and nonprofits while profiting from being in the middle. They take a cut, hold funds for weeks or months, and keep the donor data that organizations need to build and sustain relationships.

Some argue these platforms expand reach and make giving easier. They’re right that some nonprofits genuinely benefit from using them. That’s a valid choice and there’s nothing wrong with it.

But choice is the key word.

As we often say: “Nothing about us, without us.”

The issue isn’t whether platforms can be useful. It’s that GoFundMe created 1.4 million pages without asking permission. They made a choice on behalf of nonprofits that should have been ours to make.

When platforms prioritize their own growth over nonprofit consent and autonomy, they’re not solving a problem — they’re creating one.

To most donors, it feels seamless: click, confirm, done.

To nonprofits, it’s another layer of cost, delay, and disconnection.

This model doesn’t build trust.

It borrows it. Then profits from it.

What You Can Do

If you are a nonprofit: Check whether GoFundMe has created a page for your organization. They probably did. Decide whether you’re comfortable with that, and consider whether to claim it, remove it, or publicly clarify with your donors.

We weren’t comfortable, so we acted quickly to have the unauthorized page taken down.

If you are a donor: Give directly through a nonprofit’s own website and its chosen giving platform. That’s the best way to ensure your gift, your information, and your trust reach the people doing the work.

Trust and connection are our most precious resources. When you give directly, nonprofits can thank you personally, show you the impact of your gift, and invite you deeper into the mission you’re supporting.

posts.title: Philanthropy Needs a Reckoning
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: “In his eyes, generosity is an auction—and policy is the prize awarded to the highest bidder.”
posts.html:
“In his eyes, generosity is an auction—and policy is the prize awarded to the highest bidder.” — Laurene Powell Jobs, Wall Street Journal

She wrote this about Marc Benioff. But the indictment could apply to a large number of wealthy “philanthropists.”

For years, movement leaders, grassroots organizers, and we at mBOLDen Change have spoken this truth plainly: philanthropy, especially when fueled by concentrated wealth, has become a form of privatized policymaking. This is unelected power determining which communities count, which issues rise, and which solutions get funded.

In a previous piece, we challenged the premise that billionaires, celebrities, and major foundations should be praised for shaping the future of giving.

“To frame this group as the visionaries shaping the future of giving — without context, critique, or inclusion of grassroots perspectives — is to conflate visibility with vision, and power with progress.”
— mBOLDen Change

But, it’s one thing for those of us in the sector to call this out.

It’s another when a leading figure in philanthropy’s power class names the game for what it is.

The Critique Is Coming From Within

In her Wall Street Journal op-ed, Laurene Powell Jobs cut straight to the core. She cited Benioff’s own statements invoking his donations as proof of authority.

Her takeaway was blunt and damning.

“When wealth becomes a substitute for participation, giving is reduced to performance art—proof of virtue, a way to appear magnanimous while still demanding ownership. Recipients become props in donors’ narratives, rather than agents of change. Problems get framed around donors’ interests instead of people’s needs. Solutions start to serve personal recognition instead of results . . . Public institutions bend toward the priorities of the wealthy, and communities begin to measure worth in proximity to power.

The generosity that was meant to bind us together instead becomes a means of control — a way to shape policy by applause rather than by consent.”

Jobs called this dynamic “moral laundering.” She’s absolutely right.

Is she saying something novel? Not really. But she is affirming what frontline communities have understood — and experienced — for years. And when the messenger comes from inside the castle, it should be a turning point.

But we’re not naïve. Even powerful voices, don’t guarantee change.

Jobs’s critique may be extraordinary in its source, but the institutions that have ignored grassroots truth for decades are likely to just as easily ignore hers. Or worse: they’ll applaud her honesty, repost the op-ed, and change nothing.

So the question is: Will her message resonate — or will it just become a brief interlude in the performance?

Philanthropy’s Power Problem

Jobs writes that “the most effective giving empowers existing institutions, supports local leadership and creates space for communities to tackle challenges on their own terms.”

That’s not innovation.

That’s not edgy.

That’s what grassroots movements and frontline organizations have done all along, with a fraction of the resources and none of the spotlight.

In our recent critique of philanthropy’s power problem, we wrote:

“Too often, philanthropy — especially in the hands of concentrated wealth — has become a form of privatized policy-making. It’s unelected power deciding which communities matter, which issues get traction, and which solutions are deemed worthy of investment. It is profoundly undemocratic.”
— mBOLDen Change

We argued then — and still do — that real change isn’t being engineered in boardrooms or ballrooms. It’s being built on the ground by organizers, mutual aid networks, nonprofits, community leaders, and everyday people doing the work with limited resources and even less recognition.

Now Jobs is saying the same thing: that impact doesn’t come from capital. It comes from proximity, trust, and accountability to community.

So where could we all go from here? We have a few ideas:

  • Stop treating philanthropy as a substitute for public policy — and start fully and publicly funding the systems communities rely on.

  • Build a progressive tax system that moves resources to the public as they are created — not at the time, choosing and discretion of “philanthropists”

  • Invest in community-driven solutions with unrestricted dollars — no branding, no burden, no strings attached.

  • Measure impact and influence not by grants awarded or galas held, but by power shifted and communities resourced.

We’re glad Laurene Powell Jobs joined the chorus and spoke up.

Now we need a philanthropic movement that doesn’t just applaud community — it follows its lead.

posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: As the Supreme Court hears arguments that could end federal protection against racial gerrymandering, millions of minority voters are casting ballots — but their votes may soon count for less.
posts.html:
The Case That Could Change Voting Rights

As we publish this piece, the U.S. Supreme Court is set to hear arguments in Louisiana v. Callais (consolidated with Robinson v. Callais), one of the most consequential voting-rights cases in a generation. At stake is Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which has provided minority voters a powerful tool to challenge racially discriminatory redistricting plans for sixty years.

The timing is pointed. In communities across the nation, tens of millions are exercising their most fundamental democratic right and casting ballots in the 2025 off-year elections. Local elections decide how schools are run, how housing is built, how transit operates, and how much we invest in our neighbors’ well-being. They remind us that democracy is not an abstraction; it is the sum of choices made by everyday people.

But as those votes are dropped into boxes and counted in precincts, the Supreme Court is deciding whether the democratic process will still have any meaningful federal protection.

Civil Rights Law Is Being Turned on Its Head

The current dispute began with a simple fact: Louisiana’s congressional map did not reflect its citizenry. Although roughly one-third of the state’s residents are Black, the 2022 map contained only one majority-Black district out of six, effectively eroding the political power of Black voters across the state.

Black voters and civil-rights groups challenged the map under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, arguing that it denied them an equal opportunity to elect candidates of their choice. A federal court agreed. The judges found clear evidence of vote dilution and ordered the state legislature to draw a new map that included a second majority-Black district.

In response, lawmakers adopted a revised map in early 2024 that complied with the court’s order. But almost immediately, a group of white voters filed a new lawsuit, claiming that the new map was itself unconstitutional — that by considering race to remedy discrimination, the legislature had engaged in “racial gerrymandering” in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause.

Their argument turns civil-rights law on its head: that the very tools designed to correct racial inequity now constitute racial discrimination. If the Court embraces that reasoning, it could gut Section 2 or narrow it beyond recognition, erasing one of the last remaining federal safeguards against racially biased redistricting.

This is also not the first time Louisiana v. Callais has reached the high court. In its previous term, the justices weighed whether to leave in place the state’s court-ordered map but declined to rule, scheduling the case for reargument this term. In doing so, the Court agreed to take up an even higher-stakes question: whether any race-conscious effort to fix a Voting Rights Act violation violates the Fourteenth or Fifteenth Amendments to the U.S. Constitution.

Republicans in Louisiana are urging the Court to prohibit the use of race in drawing voting lines altogether, a decision that could upend decades of precedent and deliver another blow to the nation’s civil-rights architecture.

Just two years ago, the Court narrowly upheld Section 2 in an Alabama case (Allen v. Milligan), with Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joining the liberal justices to reaffirm its framework. But even then, Kavanaugh signaled that “race-based redistricting cannot extend indefinitely into the future.” Both he and Roberts, who also authored the decision ending affirmative action in college admissions in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, could again hold the balance of power in Callais.

The Silence in the Constitution

Voting is fundamental to the exercise of democracy. Many consider it the most fundamental right in a democracy. Yet, the Constitution does not actually guarantee that Americans have the right to vote. Instead it delegates election rules to the states, limiting them only through amendments that prohibit discrimination based on race, sex, or age. The framers left the franchise intentionally open-ended — a gap that, in practice, has allowed states to decide not only who votes but whose votes count.

The Voting Rights Act was meant to close that gap. Signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson in 1965, it transformed moral aspiration into enforceable law. It established pre-clearance — requiring jurisdictions with histories of discrimination to obtain federal approval before changing voting procedures — and it empowered courts to strike down racially gerrymandered maps.

“Every American citizen must have an equal right to vote,” Johnson told Congress. “There is no reason which can excuse the denial of that right.”

For nearly half a century, that promise held. Then the Roberts Court began dismantling it, piece by piece.

How the Guardrails Fell

Like dominoes falling, the sequence was deliberate and devastating.

2013 – Shelby County v. Holder invalidated the formula used to determine which jurisdictions were subject to the pre-clearance requirements of the Voting Rights Act (Section 5). Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that “things have changed in the South,” essentially deeming racial discrimination was largely a relic of the past. Within hours, Texas announced new voter-ID requirements. Other states followed with shorter early-voting windows, polling-place closures, and aggressive voter-roll purges. Nearly 1,700 polling places vanished in previously covered jurisdictions: one closing every two days.

When civil-rights groups warned that Shelby would invite a new wave of suppression, the Court’s majority replied that Section 2 remained available to challenge discriminatory practices. That assurance rings hollow now that Section 2 itself is on the chopping block.

2019 – Rucho v. Common Cause ruled that partisan gerrymandering was beyond judicial reach — a “political question” courts couldn’t touch. The distinction between racial and partisan motives was academic. In modern America, party and race often track one another. The decision blessed extreme map-drawing so long as legislators claimed partisan rather than racial intent.

After the 2020 census, Texas redrew its districts to ensure that white voters would control the majority, ultimately leading to Republicans winning 25 of the state’s 38 congressional seats in 2022.

2025 – Louisiana v. Callais — Now comes the potential final blow. Weaken federal oversight (Shelby), remove judicial remedies (Rucho), then eliminate the last enforcement mechanism. Once those guardrails are gone, states can redraw lines, purge rolls, and manipulate rules without fear of federal review.

The insidious danger lies in its appearance of legality. Nothing seems overtly violent. The forms of democracy remain intact even as their substance drains away.

When Representation Disappears

Legal scholars will debate whether Section 2 exceeds Congress’s authority or violates equal-protection principles. Those questions matter, but they obscure a simpler one: when representation disappears, whose voices will count?

If Section 2 falls, communities of color will lose the ability to challenge maps that divide and diminish them. The courts will close their doors to claims of vote dilution. State constitutions may offer some relief, but those safeguards are uneven and easily undone.

The consequences land hardest in neighborhoods whose boundaries are redrawn to split a Black community in two; in city councils that no longer mirror the demographics of the people they serve; in transit systems and housing policies shaped by representatives who no longer reflect their communities.

Congress Has the Power to Act

The Supreme Court may decide what the Voting Rights Act means, but Congress decides whether it exists. Congress has always had the power to protect the right to vote. What it has lacked is the will.

Bills to strengthen those protections have been written, introduced, and reintroduced — only to die in committee or on the Senate floor.

  • The John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act would restore pre-clearance with a modernized formula.
