  • The Freedom to Vote Act would set national standards for early voting, same-day registration, and mail-in ballots while banning partisan gerrymandering in federal elections.

  • The Deceptive Practices and Voter Intimidation Prevention Act would create penalties for disinformation campaigns.

These are not radical proposals. They are the bare minimum of a functioning democracy: the administrative equivalent of keeping the lights on. And yet, year after year, our elected leaders have allowed that light to flicker and dim.

One Person, One Vote?

The struggle over voting rights has always been about more than procedure. It is about who is seen as fully part of “We the People.” The tactics change — literacy tests and poll taxes in one era, voter-ID laws and map manipulation in another. But the underlying impulse is constant: to define citizenship and limit the exercise of voting narrowly enough to preserve power.

The demise of democracy often begins quietly — when citizens stop believing their votes and voices matter, or when that belief becomes true.

The surest way to destroy democracy is not to abolish elections but to hollow them out: to preserve the rituals of voting while stripping away the rights and safeguards that make those votes fair. We need only look to China, Russia, and other authoritarian regimes to see how this plays out. Each time the courts narrow who may vote or whose votes count, the circle of representation contracts. Each time the public shrugs, the contraction accelerates.

The right to vote — freely, fairly, and easily — has never enforced itself. It survives only through vigilance.

Sixty years ago, President Johnson addressed Congress after the violence in Selma: “It is wrong — deadly wrong — to deny any of your fellow Americans the right to vote in this country.”

That conviction became the moral foundation of the Voting Rights Act.

Today, the question before the Supreme Court (and all of us) is whether that conviction still holds.

One person, one vote.

A republic, if we can keep it.

posts.title: Hunger by Policy
posts.subtitle: When a nation expands ICE while shrinking SNAP, it’s not balancing a budget — it’s choosing control over care.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: When a nation expands ICE while shrinking SNAP, it’s not balancing a budget — it’s choosing control over care.
posts.html:
In the San Francisco Bay Area — where billion-dollar IPOs dominate headlines and grocery bills quietly break families — the cost of living has been a quiet emergency for years, now pushed to the brink by new federal cuts.

Across Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and San Francisco counties, hundreds of thousands of people rely on CalFresh, known federally as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), to keep food on the table. For many, it’s the difference between dinner and hunger.

What’s unfolding in the Bay Area is not unique; it’s a mirror of what’s happening nationwide. From rural towns to major cities, the same pattern repeats: federal retrenchment, local desperation, and an overreliance on charity to fill policy gaps. We write from here, but this story belongs to every community in America.

From New York to New Mexico, from Ohio to Oklahoma, from Mississippi to Maine, households are living under the same pattern of rising costs, shrinking support, and policies that punish poverty.

For struggling households, SNAP isn’t a luxury — it’s survival. For parents juggling multiple low-wage jobs, it means their kids don’t go to school or bed hungry. For a veteran, it’s the margin that keeps them from sliding into homelessness. For foster youth, it means stability as they make the transition to adulthood.

But soon, this basic needs program will be cut off for millions.

The Deliberate Demolition of the Safety Net

President Trump’s new spending bill, H.R. 1, makes devastating cuts to programs millions depend on. Over the next decade, it will strip $186 billion from SNAP and $1 trillion from Medicaid — a dismantling of the nation’s core safety net disguised as “fiscal reform.” These aren’t abstract numbers: they represent food, medicine and stability for millions of families already living on the edge.

View this on Substack

The local impact is staggering:

  • Santa Clara County: Up to 55,000 residents could lose food assistance

  • Alameda County: Tens of thousands more at risk (in a county where 1 in 4 people is already food-insecure)

  • Contra Costa and San Francisco Counties: Bracing for similar losses despite having some of the nation’s highest costs of living

No food bank, no matter how efficient, innovative or heroic, can absorb losses of this scale.

This is not about fiscal responsibility. This is a deliberate policy choice to punish poverty and ration dignity.

The Myth of Meritocracy

Behind these cuts lies one of America’s most enduring fictions: the myth of meritocracy — the belief that those who work hard succeed, and those who struggle simply haven’t tried hard enough. It’s a story we tell to make inequality feel deserved.

That myth underwrites every rule in this bill. It’s what allows lawmakers to call punishment “personal responsibility” and to treat poverty as a moral defect rather than a policy failure.

The new requirements expand and intensify that punitive logic:

  • People ages 18 to 64 must now document 20 hours a week of employment, volunteer service, or job training to remain eligible

  • Parents only qualify for an exemption if their children are under 14

  • Veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth —groups once recognized as vulnerable — lose their exemptions entirely

Miss the threshold for three months, and you lose your benefits for three years.

These are not bureaucratic adjustments; they are acts of erasure. Where rent consumes entire paychecks, where even full-time workers depend on food aid, the message is unmistakable: hunger has become a policy choice disguised as “fiscal responsibility.”

The Math of Economic Gaslighting

Let’s look at the numbers in the Bay Area, because they show how national policy failures play out at the local level:

In Santa Clara County, a single adult must earn around $100,000 a year to meet basic expenses. CalFresh caps eligibility just below $20,000. The average monthly benefit? $219.

That modest amount doesn’t just feed households — it sustains communities. Every dollar in SNAP benefits generates $1.54 in local economic activity, circulating through neighborhood grocers, farmers markets and small businesses. That ripple effect is true in every community across the country — but in high-cost regions like the Bay Area, it’s often the only thing holding families above water.

To call these cuts “savings” is economic gaslighting. They don’t save money; they shift the burden from the federal ledger to local food banks, counties, and the people least able to shoulder it.

The strain is already severe. Second Harvest of Silicon Valley serves more people than ever — 1 in 6 residents — distributing 106 million meals last year, a 62% increase since 2019. The Trump administration’s proposed cuts to SNAP will make that strain even worse.

Statewide, advocates warn that nearly 700,000 Californians could lose or see reductions in their benefits when H.R.1 takes effect.

This isn’t a hunger crisis waiting to happen. It’s one already here — in California and in every state where families are paying for federal neglect with empty refrigerators and impossible choices.

The Moral Calculus: What We Choose to Fund

Budgets are moral documents. They tell us what — and whom — a nation values.

While Congress dismantles programs that feed and heal, it pours unprecedented sums into enforcement and surveillance:

  • $45 billion to ICE for detention expansion

  • $30 billion for deportation operations

  • Detention capacity expanding to 100,000 beds nationwide

We are witnessing a perverse inversion of priorities: billions for cages, and cuts for classrooms, kitchens and care. We are investing more to police poverty than to prevent it.

This is not about fiscal responsibility. It’s about control — about deciding whose suffering is politically acceptable.

The Work Ahead

Widespread hunger is not an accident. It is the predictable result of decisions made by people in power. When a government expands ICE while shrinking SNAP, it is declaring that surveillance matters more than sustenance.

But here’s the other truth: we are not powerless. Ironically, surrendering to powerlessness is exactly what these policies depend on.

Across the country, food banks do the impossible every day. But they cannot replace policy. They can fill pantries, not budget holes. We need both immediate relief and systemic change.

We deserve a government that measures success not by the number of people it can detain, but by the number it can feed — one that invests in people’s capacity to thrive, not just their ability to survive.

Beyond Charity

Support for nonprofits and food banks is essential, but philanthropy is not a substitute for policy. When communities must depend on private generosity to solve hunger and poverty, it reveals just how deeply government has retreated from its responsibility to care for people.

Systemic challenges require systemic solutions. This is why our response must be twofold: build resilience locally and demand reform nationally.

Local Action: Mitigation, Not Replacement

Communities across the country are considering local tax measures to offset the cuts coming from Washington. While local revenue can soften the blow, it cannot stop the bleeding — or replace the backbone of a federal safety net decades in the making. The scale is simply too massive.

Santa Clara County’s proposed sales-tax measure (Measure A) is expected to generate hundreds of millions annually for safety-net services — significant resources, but nowhere near enough to backfill SNAP cuts and Medicaid reductions. Other Bay Area counties are drawing on previously passed tax measures to mitigate some impacts, but the gaps remain staggering.

Still, mitigation matters. Every family kept fed, every person kept housed, every gap we can close locally is worth fighting for. Raising progressive revenue at the local level is an act of resistance to federal neglect — a way for communities to say: If Washington won’t fully protect our people, we’ll do what we can.

What you can do locally:

  1. Contact your county supervisors — Tell them safety-net funding is non-negotiable and ask how they plan to address federal cuts

  2. Vote for progressive revenue measures — Support ballot initiatives that fund community care, while understanding their limitations

  3. Support local food banks — Donate, volunteer, and amplify their work. They are more strained than ever.

State-Level Advocacy

Local action must be a beginning, not an end. State legislators should champion tax reforms that restore and expand the social safety net, close corporate loopholes, and ensure those who’ve benefited most from decades of growth contribute their fair share.

California has long led the nation in innovation and inclusion. It must now lead in equity.

National Advocacy: Make Your Voice Heard

Yes, the GOP currently controls all branches of government. But participatory democracy doesn’t pause because the political winds shift — it matters most when the stakes are highest.

Why your voice matters:

  • Congressional offices track constituent calls and emails — they shape what issues get attention

  • Public pressure has stopped harmful legislation before, even in divided times

  • Your representatives need to know their constituents oppose these cuts, especially if they’re considering future votes

  • Building a record of opposition now creates accountability for future elections

Take action:

  1. Call your U.S. Representative and Senators — Tell them you oppose SNAP and Medicaid cuts in H.R. 1. Be specific: “I’m calling to urge you to oppose the cuts to SNAP and Medicaid in H.R. 1. These programs are lifelines for families in my community.”

  2. Share your story — Personal impacts matter more than statistics. If you or someone you know relies on these programs, say so.

  3. Organize with others — Join advocacy groups, attend town halls, make this a collective effort

Democracy isn’t a fair-weather activity. When the fight feels hardest is precisely when participation matters most.

We need a budget that funds care, not cruelty — one that aligns our fiscal choices with our moral ones.

So yes, support your local food bank. But, more importantly, support the public budgets and policies that make food banks less necessary. Call your representatives. Show up to city council meetings. Vote for measures that raise progressive revenue. Demand that our elected officials match their rhetoric on community with policies that keep people fed, housed, and whole.

If hunger can be written into policy, so can compassion. The choice is up to us.

posts.title: Trump’s Shutdown Is a Lose-Lose for Americans
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: The government shut down at 12:01 a.m., and while pundits tally wins and losses and headlines frame it as just another partisan standoff, the truth is this: the shutdown is a lose-lose for Americans, engineered by President Trump and his GOP allies.
posts.html:
The government shut down at 12:01 a.m., and while pundits tally wins and losses and headlines frame it as just another partisan standoff, the truth is this: the shutdown is a lose-lose for Americans, engineered by President Trump and his GOP allies.

Trump’s budget bill, passed earlier this summer, is an act of cruelty and sabotage. It would effectively end the ACA tax credits that make health insurance affordable for millions of working families. Without them, premiums are projected to more than double overnight. Add to that draconian cuts to Medicaid, and millions more will lose coverage entirely.

This isn’t abstract policy. Poverty and poor health are a vicious cycle: illness drives people deeper into debt, and financial strain fuels worse health outcomes.

Affordable healthcare and a basic safety net for all is a human right — and a line no elected leader or party should ever cross.

Yet here we are.

The Double Bind of Poverty and Health

Poverty isn’t just about the ledger — it’s about years stripped from people’s lives. It shows up in higher rates of diabetes, heart disease, asthma, and depression. It forces parents to skip medication to cover rent, or delay care until they have no choice but an emergency. And when that emergency comes, the bill can wipe out whatever fragile stability a family has left.

Unaffordable healthcare drives people into poverty. Poverty drives people into illness. It’s a double bind: a cruel trap that keeps people scrambling for survival instead of building toward stability.

Every day without affordable care means lives cut short, families bankrupted and communities left sicker and poorer.

Manufactured Crisis

And now, instead of fixing the problem, the White House is deliberately weaponizing it. Trump and his allies are holding the country hostage: either agree to slash public services, or they will be slashed anyway. It is a crisis engineered to turn basic human rights into bargaining chips.

Trump has gone further than any president before him — openly threatening to fire thousands of federal workers during the shutdown as an act of political violence. It’s a strategy of intimidation, meant to inflict maximum economic pain on everyday Americans who depend on a functioning government and political pain on opponents in Congress.

View this on Substack

This is not negotiation. It is extortion at the expense of people’s health and livelihoods.

Who Pays the Price

The bill doesn’t come due in Washington; it comes due at kitchen tables, in living rooms and in hospital waiting rooms across America — for patients whose surgeries are delayed, veterans whose benefits are interrupted, and families who lose access to food assistance or childcare. Meanwhile, politicians keep collecting their salaries while more than two million federal workers and their families watch their paychecks vanish overnight.

Every shutdown inflicts instability, insecurity and harm. When workers are furloughed, when services are suspended, when coverage is threatened, it isn’t Washington that suffers. It’s ordinary families already carrying the crushing weight of broken policy.

We Deserve Better

We deserve more than a choice between two bad options. We deserve a safety net that is not held hostage by political standoffs. We deserve a government that treats health not as a partisan concession, but as a basic human right.

Beneath the partisan drama in Washington, the real crisis will be counted in missed doctor’s visits, skipped medications, federal workers living without pay, and families pushed deeper into poverty.

As long as people’s livelihoods are treated as bargaining chips, crises like this will continue to do what poverty already does every day: strip people of health, wealth and dignity.

What We Can Do

We are not powerless.

We can call our representatives and make it clear: healthcare is not negotiable.

We can show solidarity with furloughed workers by supporting mutual aid funds and community organizations stepping in where government has walked away.

And we must refuse to normalize a system that treats survival as leverage in a political game.

This moment is not just about one shutdown. It’s about every time leaders choose political violence or weaponize the legislative process at the expense of people’s lives. They count on our silence. We must not give it to them.

posts.title: Erasing the Data: Trump’s War on All of Us
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: Blink and you’ll miss it.
posts.html:
Blink and you’ll miss it.

The Trump administration has just canceled the nation’s most important survey of hunger in America, a study that has been the most reliable measure of food insecurity since the mid-1990s.

But this wasn’t just a tally of hunger; it was a map of the intersections of poverty. Economist Craig Gundersen, for example, used this dataset to uncover how food insecurity overlaps with disability, health status, and regional inequities. His work, along with that of countless other scholars and public health experts, underscored why the survey mattered: without the study, the nation loses a compass for gauging how its most vulnerable citizens are faring.

The cancellation comes on the heels of legislation signed by Trump over the summer that slashed funding for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and tightened work requirements. Now it will be harder to prove what those cuts mean for families. As Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutrition professor at the University of North Carolina, warns:

“Why would you not want to measure it? I think the only reason why you wouldn’t measure it is if you were planning to cut food assistance, because it basically allows you to pretend like we don’t have this food insecurity problem.”

This isn’t policy as usual. This is policy by erasure.

The War on Data

The food insecurity survey is just the latest casualty in Trump’s broader assault on reality. Blink again, and you’ll notice entire datasets, websites, and offices have disappeared.

Over the past eight months, federal agencies have purged data, reshaped methodologies, and defunded core reporting tools. A few examples:

Census distortions designed to undercount immigrants and low-income households. In his first term, Trump pushed to add a citizenship question to the census — an effort widely understood as a bid to intimidate immigrant families and drive down participation. The Supreme Court blocked the move, but the damage was done: the political debate created a chilling effect. The Bureau later estimated it undercounted the Hispanic or Latino population by 4.99% and the Black or African American population by 3.30% in the 2020 Census.

Now, in Trump 2.0, the plan is even starker: exclude undocumented immigrants from the census count altogether. That single act would radically reshape congressional representation and strip billions in funding from communities already shortchanged.

Environmental rollbacks erased climate and justice data at record pace. In its first 100 days, Trump 2.0 made 70% more changes to government environmental websites than in his first administration. The targets were clear: environmental justice, climate change, and diversity, equity, and inclusion. Within days of taking office, the White House’s Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool was removed, along with nine other agency tools that identified disadvantaged communities.

Just this month, the Environmental Protection Agency moved to end the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, which since 2010 has required thousands of coal plants, refineries, and industrial facilities to disclose their emissions of carbon dioxide, methane, and other heat-trapping gases. The program tracks data from roughly 8,000 of the nation’s largest polluters — data that has guided federal climate policy, fulfilled U.N. reporting obligations under the Paris Agreement, and even allowed local communities to monitor nearby facilities. Ending it would gut one of the federal government’s only reliable tools for measuring and reducing emissions.

This level of erasure of environmental justice information is unprecedented. Without these tools and sites, communities lose evidence of disproportionate pollution burdens, scientists lose vital climate data, and the public loses access to the information it needs to hold government accountable.

“When we don’t measure things, it makes it much harder to claim that there is a problem and that the government has some kind of responsibility to help alleviate it. Measuring itself is a political act with political consequences. And clearly the Trump administration does not want to do anything to alleviate a problem like climate change.”

— Sarah Pralle, Associate Professor of Political Science at Syracuse University, as quoted in the New York Times

Education data cuts hollowed out accountability. Under Trump’s direction, the Department of Education scaled back the Civil Rights Data Collection, making it harder to see how schools discipline students by race, disability status, or language background. Reports required under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) were delayed or narrowed. In practice, this means fewer windows into whether children with disabilities are receiving the supports federal law guarantees.

The rollbacks didn’t stop there. Understaffing and shifting priorities at the Office for Civil Rights slowed the release of key datasets on everything from sexual harassment to restraint and seclusion of students with special needs. Data on English-language learners was pared back, obscuring whether schools are meeting their obligation to educate immigrant and bilingual students. And while school boards spar over “critical race theory,” the federal government is quietly dismantling the very numbers that prove racial disparities exist in the first place.

These aren’t abstract shifts. Without this data, families cannot prove discrimination, advocates cannot press for enforcement, and Congress cannot measure whether billions in federal education dollars are reaching the children who need them most. The result is a classroom where inequity becomes invisible by design — and if you can’t count it, you can’t fix it.

Public health blind spots erased trusted medical information. Soon after Trump took office, federal health officials removed webpages and data on topics ranging from pregnancy risks to opioid-use disorder to the AIDS epidemic. The purge followed an executive order directing agencies to stop using the term “gender” in federal policies and documents, part of an effort the administration cast as ending “gender ideology.” Doctors and public health advocates called it government overreach.

“This was trusted health information that vanished in a blink of an eye — resources that, among other things, physicians rely on to manage patients’ health conditions and overall care,” said Dr. John Bramhall of the Washington State Medical Association, one of the lead plaintiffs in a lawsuit that forced the government to restore more than 100 sites.

But the data erasures go well beyond health websites. At the CDC, layoffs have gutted the National Center for Injury Prevention and Control, which maintains statistics on car crashes, drownings, gun violence, and traumatic brain injuries. Trump’s budget would eliminate its funding altogether, threatening the National Violent Death Reporting System — a database used to design suicide prevention programs, evaluate law enforcement use of force, and identify where to intervene before tragedies occur.

Each of these cuts carries real consequences: physicians lose tools for patient care, scientists lose data to track crises, and communities lose the ability to push for prevention and accountability. While lawsuits have forced the restoration of some information, the larger pattern is clear — this administration is dismantling the very infrastructure that keeps the public safe.

Trump Logic: If the numbers don’t exist, the harm doesn’t either.

The Logic of Erasure

The logic of erasing data is as blunt as it is brutal.

If you don’t measure hunger, you can slash food aid with fewer headlines.

If you don’t count immigrants, you can strip their rights with less backlash.

If you don’t track pollution, you can greenlight corporate polluters without protest.

If you don’t monitor disability, you can cut services without consequence.

Data is the connective tissue between lived experience and collective action. It gives advocates evidence. It gives communities a voice. It gives policymakers the tools to make informed decisions. And it gives the public a gauge to hold those in power accountable.

Erasing data does not erase the problem. It erases the people.

Taking a Hammer to Shared Reality

Data holds up a mirror, offering an unflinching look at our own reality. At their best, numbers, surveys and datasets allow us to see how we’re doing, even when the reflection is uncomfortable. But distort them, and they become a funhouse mirror that warps truth to serve bad actors in power. Remove them, and we lose more than transparency — we lose the ability to govern, shape policy, and allocate resources from a shared reality.

The consequences are playing out like a train wreck in real time. Without food insecurity data, it will be harder to track the human toll of SNAP cuts. Without environmental reporting, communities will be slower to detect toxic exposure. Without census accuracy, representation and resources will skew even further away from those who need them most.

This isn’t a battle over spreadsheets; it’s a fight for a shared reality — and right now, reality itself is losing.

Protecting the People’s Data

The Trump administration can distort or delete datasets, but it doesn’t have a monopoly on data collection — and it doesn’t own our shared reality.

Independent researchers, nonprofits, journalists, and communities are building their own forms of data collection and public accountability. Initiatives like The Impact Project track how policy changes affect families in real time, producing state-by-state data on everything from tax credits to food assistance. Environmental watchdogs like the Environmental Data & Governance Initiative preserve disappearing climate and pollution data. Civic efforts such as the Data Rescue Project mobilize volunteers to archive vulnerable federal datasets, ensuring that even if government websites go dark, the underlying information remains publicly accessible.

Yet these efforts are underfunded, fragmented, and vulnerable to attack. A handful of civil society organizations cannot carry the burden of transparency for an entire nation.

View this on Substack

What we need is a movement for data justice:

  • Protect independent data collection and make it publicly accessible.

  • Fund community-driven research that centers lived experience.

  • Demand transparency as a democratic right, not a bureaucratic luxury.

  • Build bridges between academic research, grassroots organizing, and policy change.

The Stakes

We live in an era of cascading, interconnected crises: hunger, climate change, inequality, democratic backsliding. None exists in isolation; each compounds the others. And in every case, data isn’t peripheral — it’s central. It’s how we know who is most at risk, which interventions are working, and where resources must go.

By dismantling data systems, the Trump administration isn’t just suppressing numbers. It’s dismantling our ability to respond to crisis itself.

At a human level, data signals who this country chooses to see, how they are seen — and therefore who is valued. Erase the numbers, and you erase people’s place in the national story.

Ultimately, this is about making inequity harder to see, harder to name, harder to fight.

That’s why this must be resisted — ferociously, collectively, and without delay. Because when the data disappears, so do the people. And when the people disappear from view, injustice doesn’t just thrive in the dark. It metastasizes.

posts.title: Words Hold Power
posts.subtitle: How the Language We Choose Shapes Politics and Possibility
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: How the Language We Choose Shapes Politics and Possibility
posts.html:
Words don’t just describe reality; they create it. They shape how we perceive the world and influence our feelings about who counts, what is imaginable, and which futures feel possible. Across history, language has been used to justify conquest, entrench inequality and normalize exclusion. The American right wing has mastered this, spending years turning everyday speech into a weapon: rebranding anti-choice politics as “pro-life,” cloaking censorship in “parents’ rights,” recasting multiracial democracy as a battle against “wokeness,” and labeling immigrant neighbors as “illegals,” “animals,” or an “invasion.” None of this is accidental. It’s a deliberate strategy to set the frame before the rest of us have even entered the conversation.

If we aren’t defining the terms, we’re living (no, trapped) inside someone else’s story. To get out, we have to change the narrative and seize the power of language — not just to fight back, but to tell the story of the world we're inviting others to build alongside us.

How Language Shapes Reality

Language is the scaffolding of society. It shapes who is seen as fully human, what harms are tolerated, and which solutions are deemed just and possible.

This truth is painfully visible today. Led by Trump, the right has weaponized everyday speech, deploying a narrative of grievance and exclusion. Labeling people “illegals” shifts the frame from a broken immigration system to individual blame. Rebranding bureaucratic checks and balances as the “deep state” distorts how we think about government and freedom. Declaring that “all lives matter” sounds neutral and moral while stripping away the very context of racism and inequality it seeks to erase.

These words aren’t accidental. They are chosen to provoke emotion, drive policy momentum, and ultimately shape whose dignity will be honored — or denied.

As linguist John McWhorter recently noted in The New York Times, “Even Trump’s most positive-sounding coinages are acts of a certain kind of verbal aggression.” The point is not just rhetoric — it’s domination. Calling a bill “Big and Beautiful” or renaming the Department of Defense the “Department of War” isn’t random branding. It’s a linguistic power play, designed to frame opponents as weak, “wokey,” or irrelevant before the debate has even started.

But the power of language works both ways. It has also been the spark for movements that expanded rights, rebuilt the moral center of public life, and redrew the boundaries of the possible.

The fight against slavery was waged not just with guns and petitions but with words. Abolitionists described slavery as “man stealing,” “sin,” and “a crime against humanity.” Slaveholders, in turn, cloaked it in the language of “states’ rights” and “property.” The battle over words was inseparable from the battle over laws.

During the civil rights movement of the 1960s, leaders invoked the language of freedom, dignity, and equality — values embedded in America’s founding documents but denied to millions. That framing let their demands resonate not only as policy but as fulfillment of America’s supposed promise.

During the AIDS crisis, activists transformed a stigmatized “gay plague” into “people with AIDS,” paired with the blunt moral clarity of Silence = Death. Words opened the space for research dollars, treatment, and human solidarity.

When Nelson Mandela and the ANC were branded as “terrorists,” it justified imprisonment and isolation. When they were reframed as “freedom fighters,” the ground shifted. Legitimacy followed language.

Over and over again, history shows us how language shapes social values.

A Narrative of Asymmetrical Violence

We don’t have to look far to see these dynamics. Consider the contrast between two recent tragedies. When Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman was murdered, the Trump administration and its allies refused to call it political extremism. They downplayed it, treating the killing as an isolated crime despite evidence to the contrary. Yet after conservative activist Charlie Kirk was murdered, those same voices immediately branded it “left-wing extremism,” amplified the story across the media, and demanded crackdowns on their opponents.

The difference is not about evidence. It is about the frame.

By refusing to name right-wing violence while loudly labeling any act of violence against conservatives as political, the Trump administration is signaling to the public whose lives matter, whose pain deserves outrage, and whose violence gets normalized. This asymmetry is not accidental — it is strategy.

We saw the same pattern after the January 6th attack on the U.S. Capitol. Armed mobs stormed the seat of government, chanted about hanging the Vice President, and forced members of Congress to flee for their lives. Yet Trump and his allies resisted calling it an insurrection or domestic terrorism. Instead, they reframed it as a “protest,” casting its participants as “patriots” or even “tourists.” That rebranding wasn’t trivial. It sought to strip the event of its violence and recast it as legitimate dissent, softening public outrage and muddying accountability. Once again, the language here was used not to describe reality but to manipulate it.

What the Research Shows

The power of language is not just theory; the impact is measurable. Public opinion research consistently shows how the terms we use shape what people believe and what policies they are willing to support.

The debate over the Affordable Care Act (ACA) provides a perfect example. Despite being the same law, polls from Morning Consult found that a third of Americans were unaware that the ACA and Obamacare were one and the same. The study also found that Republicans were significantly more likely to disapprove when the law was called "Obamacare" as opposed to the "Affordable Care Act." This wasn't a difference in policy preference, but a difference in emotional reaction to a word. The name alone, a strategic branding choice by opponents, was enough to polarize people and change their minds.

View this on Substack

The same pattern shows up in immigration. When poll questions about immigration use the term “undocumented” or “unauthorized” immigrant instead of “illegal immigrant,” support for a pathway to citizenship often rises by double digits. The term “illegal” frames individuals as criminals, while “undocumented” frames them as people navigating a complex system.

The same principle applies to economic policy. “Tax relief” frames taxes as a burden, casting cuts for corporations and the wealthy as liberation. “Investments in our communities” frames public spending on schools, healthcare, and infrastructure as a shared good. This is supported by a FrameWorks Institute study that found people were far more likely to support public services when they were described as “investments.”

These aren’t just semantic shifts. They alter what people fight for and what they will allow to be dismantled.

A recent comparative analysis of campaign speeches in the U.S., France, and Italy underscores the point: right-wing populists don’t succeed because they own a magic vocabulary. They succeed because they tell a simple, repeatable story: the “good people” versus “corrupt elites” and “dangerous others.” Their mainstream opponents, by contrast, too often retreat into abstractions that blur actors, stakes, and outcomes.

In public persuasion, clarity and a compelling story will always beat a data table.

The Biggest Mistake We Make

The right-wing is winning because they are telling a story of the world they want — however cruel. To inspire, we must tell the story of what we love and the world we are ready to build: one of solidarity, justice, and shared possibility.

Too often, we play defense and define ourselves by what we’re not: not extremists, not authoritarians, not Trump. But absence is not a vision. Negation is not a story. People want to know the future they’re being asked to build. Evidence matters, but facts and evidence alone rarely move hearts. A sense of comradery, rooted in shared values, perspectives and experiences, is what does. This is why storytelling is one of the strongest vehicles we have for shaping and building collective vision.

The right’s archetypes — “welfare queen,” “dangerous immigrant,” “patriotic soldier” — are sticky because they locate villains, victims, and heroes in a single breath. They tell us who belongs, who threatens, and who redeems. Each story reinforces a larger argument: America is under siege, order must be restored, and exclusion is the only path to safety.

We, too, have used powerful frameworks to shape a collective vision. The immigrant rights movement recast young undocumented immigrants as “Dreamers” — innocent, striving, deeply American, and victims of a broken system who became heroes through their persistence. During the pandemic, the language of frontline and essential workers elevated nurses, grocery clerks, and delivery drivers into everyday heroes holding society together, while corporate greed and government neglect were cast as villains. And the Occupy movement gave us the 99%, a rallying cry that united ordinary people as the vast majority struggling for fairness against a privileged, extractive elite. Together, these archetypes offer a story of belonging and solidarity: a society where dignity is not conditional, opportunity is not rationed, and power comes from the many, not the few.

The challenge is not finding stories. It is weaving them into a shared vision. That is more than moral clarity. It is political strategy.

Everyday Actions: How We Shift the Narrative

Narrative change is not only the work of leaders or organizations. It is a collective practice. Every conversation, every social media post, every story told at a family table either reinforces the old narrative or seeds a new one. At mBOLDen Change, here is what we are doing — and what you can do too:

  • Challenge harmful words. Words like “illegal alien” or “unskilled worker” are designed to demean. Replace them with language that reinforces dignity.

  • Share your own story. Authentic stories build connection in ways statistics never can. It might be your family’s journey of migration, but it could just as easily be about holding two jobs, caring for a loved one, or organizing in your neighborhood. People connect to people. When we share the struggles and hopes that shape our lives, we invite others to see themselves in the story and to imagine a different future alongside us.

  • Refuse false choices. Don’t accept “security or compassion,” “economy or justice.” These are traps, not truths.

  • Amplify community-led groups. The most powerful narratives come from lived experience. When we amplify voices at the grassroots, we challenge elite spin with truth from those closest to the challenges.

  • Repeat values. Repetition builds reality. Anchor conversations in dignity, fairness, and humanity — and keep repeating them until they become the chorus of common ground.

The Real Stakes

The battle over language isn’t about clever spin; it’s about power. When the right brands refugees as “invaders,” it builds support for bans, walls and camps. When we reframe healthcare as a human right, we build momentum toward universal coverage. Words open or close political pathways before laws are even written.

Trump knows words matter. That’s why he renames, reframes, and repeats until his language becomes common. The question is whether the rest of us will meet that challenge with the discipline, vision and clarity this moment demands.

Language shapes power, possibility and belonging. Let’s choose with intent — because the future we inherit may very well depend on the words we choose today.

posts.title: Hardwired Inequity: How Big Tech’s AI Arms Race Puts Patient Care at Risk
posts.author: Minh Ngo
posts.excerpt: With the right guardrails and regulation, AI tools could support breakthroughs in healthcare: from faster research to more personalized care.
posts.html:
With the right guardrails and regulation, AI tools could support breakthroughs in healthcare: from faster research to more personalized care. But that promise will be squandered if we fail to put patient safety, equity, and care above profit.

Even the people who build AI tools are worried about the race to adopt them. A manager at an AI lab at a major medical institution recently shared a concern with me: their team is one of the few prioritizing ethical development and patient-centric design — putting them at odds with an industry-wide race to be first to market. That conversation stayed with me because it crystallized something essential: AI itself isn’t the problem. The problem is the human choice to put speed and profit above care.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, a long-hidden flaw in an everyday medical tool — the pulse oximeter — was brutally exposed. These small devices, clipped to a patient’s finger to measure oxygen, were consistently less accurate on darker skin. This wasn’t new; researchers had documented it decades earlier, but the design flaw lingered in millions of devices. When COVID hit, skewed readings fed into hospital triage algorithms that decided who received supplemental oxygen and who was turned away. The result was predictable and devastating: Black patients with dangerously low oxygen levels were more likely to be undertreated.

The pulse oximeter was one of the most visible examples of how design bias turns deadly. But it was not unique. For decades, White male participants have been overrepresented in medical research. Drugs, vaccines, and treatments have often been tested primarily on this group, leaving women and communities of color underrepresented in clinical trials. The result is predictable: therapies that are less effective or riskier when prescribed more broadly. Women, for example, metabolize some drugs differently, which has led to serious side effects that never surfaced in trials dominated by men.

These gaps don’t just live in the past; they still shape today’s standards of care. Now imagine that history of bias scaled across every corner of healthcare — not just in one device or a handful of trials, but in the AI systems hospitals, labs, and policymakers are choosing to adopt to guide diagnosis, treatment, and access to care. That is the future the Trump administration and Big Tech are building. The rest of us? We are sleepwalking (nope, speedwalking) into it.

The question isn’t whether AI will be integrated into healthcare, but whether decision-makers will hardwire the biases of the past and present into the future of care.

The AI Action Plan: A Health Policy in Disguise

The Trump administration’s AI Action Plan barely mentions healthcare, but its impact could reshape the future of our health system more than any policy in a generation. Released in July, the plan calls for a “try-first” culture enabled by “regulatory sandboxes” — environments where companies can rapidly test AI tools while bypassing rigorous oversight. The plan promises to fast-track “private-sector-led innovation” by requiring AI tools to exclude established social determinants of health like race, gender, and environment, which it calls “ideological.” It even recommends revising the AI Risk Management Framework to explicitly eliminate references to misinformation, Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion, and climate change.

In practice, this pressures developers to strip out the very factors that shape real health outcomes. While the administration rolls back oversight and narrows which data are allowed to count, any model that dares to recognize the social determinants of health could be branded political — and buried.

This is not happening in a vacuum. The administration has already purged CDC websites, halted NIH funding for projects tied to diversity, and granted political appointees the power to cancel research grants that don’t “demonstrably advance the President’s policy priorities.” These deliberate policy choices are shaping which data gets collected, which research gets funded, and what kinds of AI tools will be built. The selective erasure of data isn’t symbolic: it’s structural. And it is hardwiring bias into healthcare’s future.

Silicon Valley Breaks Things

Silicon Valley’s “move fast and break things” mindset has infected the hallowed halls of medicine. From Stanford to Harvard to Mayo, elite medical institutions are in an AI arms race. Venture dollars and hospital budgets flow toward the labs and administrators who embrace AI the fastest, not those who do the hard work of interrogating bias and safeguarding patient care.

This is not “AI taking over healthcare.” It is medical leaders, academic institutions, and decision-makers deciding to roll out unproven systems at scale. They are choosing to treat questions of privacy, bias, and patient well-being as hurdles for later. But healthcare is not software. You cannot beta-test with human bodies. Once a flawed tool is integrated into hospital protocols, its blind spots don’t just linger — they become practice. Then policy. Then a part of law.

Garbage In, Bias Out

AI is only as good as the data we feed it. That’s data science 101. But when our government narrows what counts as valid research — when race, gender, and community-level data are stripped from official statistics — the “garbage in” doesn’t just produce sloppy outputs. It produces health misinformation disguised as medical objectivity.

Recent studies have shown how dangerous this can be. One AI model confidently hallucinated a nonexistent body part. Others fabricated citations or offered treatment recommendations that contradicted evidence-based practice. Researchers at Mount Sinai found that a single misleading input could send chatbots spiraling into confident but false advice.

These errors don’t happen in a vacuum. They are not the fault of an inevitable technology. They are the direct result of human choices to ignore safeguards, to adopt faster than they regulate, to treat bias as an acceptable tradeoff for speed.

Human providers are biased too. Women’s pain is dismissed more often than men’s, and some medical professionals still falsely believe Black patients feel less pain. But AI adds a dangerous twist: it takes these existing biases and wraps them in a veneer of objective truth. When a large language model generates a diagnosis or treatment plan, the process is a black box. The biases shaping its outputs are invisible to both provider and patient. Worse, those outputs then feed back into training data, reinforcing the very inequities they produced. Bias in, bias out — then warped and folded back in again. A feedback loop that turns misinformation into a treatment plan, making inequity self-reinforcing, scalable, and nearly impossible to root out.

But once again, the responsibility doesn’t lie with AI. It lies with the institutions and decision-makers choosing to deploy it. It’s Big Tech and medical institutions integrating black-box systems without demanding transparency. It’s policymakers declining to require audits or bias disclosures. AI systems aren’t hardwiring inequities into healthcare — they are.

The Choice is Ours: Build Care or Hardwire Harm

By 2024, two-thirds of physicians were already using AI in their practice, a 78% jump from the year before. Soon, not using AI could be seen as malpractice. That means whatever biases are baked into these systems will no longer remain at the margins. They will become embedded in healthcare itself.

If the Trump administration succeeds in narrowing health data to fit its political ideology, and if Big Tech succeeds in commercializing biased AI tools at breakneck speed, we risk building a healthcare system that cannot see the full humanity of its patients. Patients of color misdiagnosed. Women’s symptoms dismissed. Immigrants erased from datasets entirely. And all of it presented as “objective truth.”

We’ve seen this movie before. When bias is embedded into healthcare, it becomes practice. Practice becomes policy. Policy becomes law. The AI Action Plan isn’t just about technology; it’s about who gets counted, who gets care, and who gets left behind.

If we want a health system that serves everyone, we must demand stronger regulation.

Treat AI tools like medical devices, with rigorous safety trials and oversight. Invest in equitable data, undo the rollbacks on research into health disparities, and expand datasets that reflect the full diversity of patients. Require transparency and accountability, including disclosure of training data and bias audits. And most importantly, amplify community voice — ensuring patients, especially from marginalized groups, have a say in how AI is built and deployed.

The promise of AI in healthcare is real. And, so is the peril. Left unchecked, it won’t just mirror inequities, it will automate them. But the real threat to patient care isn’t AI itself; it’s institutions, policymakers, Big Tech, and medical professionals choosing speed and profit over patient safety and community care.

Silicon Valley’s mantra has been “move fast and break things.”

In healthcare, what breaks is people.

Series Note

At mBOLDen Change, we believe our policies and systems should advance social equity and the common good. That includes fighting for technology that serves people, not profit. In this piece, we call out the ways medical institutions, Big Tech, policymakers and other decision-makers are rushing AI into healthcare without safeguards.

This article is the third in our ongoing series on the impact of AI on vulnerable communities, nonprofit systems, and the future of equity. If you missed the earlier posts, you can read them here: ‘What Does It Mean To Be Human In The Age Of AI’ and ‘Draining Vulnerable Communities To Feed The AI Race’. Stay tuned for our next installment, where we’ll continue to expose risks and lift up alternatives that put people, not profit, at the center.

posts.title: The Philanthropy Paradox: How Billionaires Grow Richer While “Giving It Away”
posts.subtitle: The Giving Pledge promised to redistribute fortunes. Instead, it exposed how philanthropy entrenches inequality.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: The Giving Pledge promised to redistribute fortunes. Instead, it exposed how philanthropy entrenches inequality.
posts.html:
Fifteen years after pledging to give away half their wealth, America’s billionaires are richer than ever.

According to a recent report from the Institute for Policy Studies (IPS), of the original 57 U.S. Giving Pledge signatories from 2010, 32 didn’t just remain billionaires — their combined net worth has grown by 283%. Adjusted for inflation, that’s still a staggering 166% increase.

Think about it: in the same decade they were celebrated for “giving their wealth away,” they accumulated more wealth than ever. Meanwhile, nonprofits scrape by while billions of dollars sit idle in philanthropic holding pens.

This isn’t generosity. It’s wealth preservation wrapped in moral theater.

The Real Divide: Wealth vs. Income

The biggest lie exposed by the Giving Pledge is the same lie that has underpinned inequality across America: the myth of meritocracy.

View this on Substack

More than 90% of us live off income: wages, salaries, maybe some modest returns on retirement accounts. Meanwhile, the ultra-wealthy live off assets: stock, real estate, and business holdings whose values soar even as they sleep. Their fortunes don’t come from work but from assets that swell tax-deferred, while the rest of us pay steeper taxes on every dollar we earn.

The “giving” barely dents their wealth, because the growth of their assets far outpaces the amount of their donations. Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, for instance, pledged to give away half their fortune. Since then, their net worth has skyrocketed more than 4,000%. They will never be able to give money away as fast as they make it.

For working people, this kind of system is unfathomable. We don’t have billions in stock appreciating while we sleep. We don’t get to park money in tax shelters that let us decide later — or never — when our communities benefit.

The Systemic Scam

Most people think of giving as a direct act: you donate money, and a charity uses it immediately to do good work. But for the ultra-wealthy, it often works differently. Their “giving” is usually a multi-step process. First, they move money into a philanthropic intermediary vehicle like a private foundation or a donor-advised fund (DAF). Only then does the money begin its journey toward an actual working charity — if it makes it there at all.

When the wealthy move money or assets into these vehicles, they secure massive tax breaks up front and reap public praise. But that doesn’t mean the money is helping anyone. According to the IPS report, of the estimated $206 billion original Pledgers have given to date, roughly 80% went into their private foundations, where they retain control and where funds can sit for years. And the billions shifted into DAFs? They never have to be distributed at all.

DAFs and private foundations are the linchpin of this system:

  • Private foundations let billionaires lock in deductions, control the assets, and “pay out” as little as 5% a year. The rest of the fortune stays invested, compounding indefinitely.

  • DAFs go even further. Donors get the full tax deduction immediately and have zero payout requirement. The money can sit there indefinitely, managed by big financial firms that take their fees while communities wait.

It’s a game of musical chairs. Assets shift from one account to another — from private foundations to DAFs, and even from a DAF to another DAF — where the donation can sit indefinitely with no payout requirement. All the while, the wealthy collect social capital for “giving,” even when very little actually gets distributed.

Here’s the reality: even when billionaires genuinely intend to give it all away — the entire premise of the Giving Pledge — the math works against them. The IPS report found that only one of the living 2010 U.S. Pledgers has technically fulfilled their pledge. Of the 22 Pledgers who have died, only one gave his entire fortune away.

This isn’t about insincerity or villainy. It’s about structure. Under today’s rules, compounding capital outpaces philanthropy every time — and it’s not even close. Which is why philanthropy, as we know it, doesn’t challenge inequality. It entrenches it.

Beyond Philanthropy

What the Giving Pledge ultimately proves is not just that philanthropy can’t keep up — but that it was never designed to. The pace of wealth accumulation under our economic and tax system virtually guarantees that fortunes grow faster than they can be given away. That isn’t a personal failing; it’s structural.

The solution isn’t waiting for the wealthy to voluntarily divest. It’s building a progressive tax system that prevents this kind of hoarding in the first place and ensures resources flow to the public as they are created — not decades later at the mercurial discretion of “philanthropists.”

Ultimately, philanthropy can never substitute for fair tax policy or public investment. It was never designed to — and it never will.

posts.title: Mexico Is Reducing Poverty. America Is Criminalizing It.
posts.author: Minh Ngo
posts.excerpt: Reading this Guardian piece about Mexico’s historic gains in reducing poverty got me thinking about a recent conversation with a friend, who shared their parent’s deep skepticism toward people receiving public benefits — an attitude I’ve heard many times before: that poverty is a personal failing, and help should be rationed.
posts.html:
Reading this Guardian piece about Mexico’s historic gains in reducing poverty got me thinking about a recent conversation with a friend, who shared their parent’s deep skepticism toward people receiving public benefits — an attitude I’ve heard many times before: that poverty is a personal failing, and help should be rationed.

That skepticism is more than cultural; it’s baked into policy. In the U.S., poverty is often demeaned or outright criminalized — as the recent homeless sweeps in D.C make clear. And, under the Trump administration, even the most basic supports now come with new barriers and conditions, forcing people to jump through hoops for help — if they qualify at all.

By contrast, Mexico has taken the opposite approach, treating support as a basic obligation of the state. And, here’s where America runs into another obstacle: the deeply ingrained belief that our problems are unique, and therefore unsolvable by looking abroad. The U.S. has always resisted learning from other nations’ solutions.

Perhaps the only thing more deeply embedded in the American psyche than the “bootstraps” myth is the idea of ”exceptionalism.”

For many, a foreign example is not just irrelevant — it’s unthinkable. Today, that resistance has devolved into something darker: open hostility toward immigrants themselves. I’ll spend more time on that in a future piece. For now, back to Mexico and what we can learn from our southern neighbor.

And, no, America is not Mexico — or Europe — where the U.S. already lags behind on measures like poverty and social mobility. But that’s exactly why Mexico’s story matters. It shows what’s possible when a government begins by putting the dignity of its poorest citizens first. That choice is worth paying attention to — and worth emulating.

Por el bien de todos, primero los pobres.

In Mexico, between 2018 and 2024, nearly 13.4 million people were lifted out of poverty — a 26% reduction — thanks to a slate of policies under former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador (AMLO). The tools were simple but powerful: raising the general minimum wage from 88.36 pesos in 2018 to 278.80 pesos by 2024 — more than tripling it — while also expanding pensions for seniors, creating stipends for young apprentices and investing in rural farmers.

These weren’t pilot projects or temporary “stimulus” checks. They are structural, nationwide commitments to put money directly in people’s hands. Families used that support to pay rent, put food on the table, and sustain small businesses.

This wasn’t just economic policy; it was a return to a core tenet of Mexico’s political identity, one that had been sidelined for decades in favor of a market-first approach. At the heart of this shift was a belief that the state has a responsibility to ensure social well-being. Or as López Obrador declared in the slogan that defined his presidency: “Por el bien de todos, primero los pobres” — For the good of all, first the poor.

That commitment is rooted in history. Mexico’s 1917 Constitution was revolutionary for its time, enshrining social rights for all citizens, including the right to education, land, and labor protections. This historical backdrop underscores why today’s gains resonate so deeply.

Now, President Claudia Sheinbaum has pledged to continue along this path, carrying forward the agenda of the so-called “Fourth Transformation” and sustaining the social policies that helped deliver these historic reductions in poverty.

View this on Substack

Not a Perfect Story

Of course, progress is never seamless. Regional disparities remain stark: while northern states surged ahead, southern states like Chiapas and Guerrero lagged behind. Critics argue that these historic gains in poverty reduction have come at a cost. The focus on direct cash transfers and pensions has led to a significant defunding of other social services, particularly in healthcare, where the number of people without access more than doubled — from 20.1 million in 2018 to 50.4 million in 2022.

The challenges extend beyond social policy. AMLO’s signature project, the Mayan Train, became a flashpoint, drawing criticism from environmentalists, indigenous leaders, and NGOs who argue that high-biodiversity sites and indigenous territories are being put at risk without meaningful consultation. When civil society groups sought to defend these rights, they faced dismissive processes and direct attacks, with the president accusing them of acting on behalf of foreign cabals rather than their own communities. Such rhetoric, combined with broader assaults on foreign-funded NGOs and a free press, has raised alarms about the erosion of democratic institutions and the narrowing of civic space.

The reality is that no society overcomes inequality in a single sweep; progress takes time — often generations. Just look at the U.S. for proof of the ebbs, flows and backsliding. Looking ahead, the question is whether Mexico can sustain its gains while addressing these shortcomings. While these challenges don’t erase the progress, they remind us that stability at scale requires more than short-term wins: it requires strong democratic institutions and a commitment to ensuring that progress reaches everyone.

A Contrast with the U.S.

Mexico is proving poverty can be reduced; America, meanwhile, is choosing policies that make it worse. Our politics are shaped by a narrative of merit — the belief that human dignity must be earned. Under the Trump administration, cuts to Medicaid, restrictions on food assistance, and the criminalization of homelessness all send a clear signal about whose humanity is expendable.

Policy choices can transform life from constant crisis to stability and dignity. Mexico has shown that by making a comprehensive investment in workers — through higher wages, universal pensions, and direct support for young people and farmers — families can move beyond survival toward stability. Beyond the economic gains, this approach has produced measurable improvements in well-being: greater food security, stronger safety nets and more dignified living conditions. In the U.S., by contrast, the basic conditions of dignity are being treated as negotiable, rather than as the foundation of a just society. Mexico’s approach flips this by treating a baseline of security as a universal responsibility.

What America Could Learn From Mexico

Mexico’s story isn’t about perfection, nor is it a blueprint. It’s about possibility — and about choices. It shows what can happen when a nation makes poverty eradication a priority. Poverty may also be shaped by global forces — economic shocks, climate crises, migration — but its severity at home reflects national political will.

For those of us in the U.S. fighting for equity, this isn’t about importing a foreign model. It’s about reckoning with our own history of successes and failures, interrogating our values, and challenging why we continue to treat human dignity as conditional.

At its core, Mexico’s example is less about specific programs and more about values. It demonstrates what’s possible when the economic security of the most vulnerable is treated as the starting point of governance, not an afterthought. America today shows us the cost of treating dignity and stability as negotiable.

The question is not whether we can afford to end poverty, but whether we have the imagination and courage to make stability and dignity the floor of a just society — not the ceiling.

posts.title: Cash Aid Isn’t the Ceiling. It’s Where a Just Society Begins.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: In the world’s wealthiest country, millions still face an impossible choice: pay the electric bill or put food on the table.
posts.html:
In the world’s wealthiest country, millions still face an impossible choice: pay the electric bill or put food on the table. This is the quiet crisis driving the case for cash aid — one that the recent New York Times piece, headlined 'Study May Undercut Idea That Cash Payments to Poor Families Help Child Development,' entirely overlooks.

The article analyzed the Baby’s First Years study, a rigorous look at whether monthly cash payments improve measures like pre-literacy, executive function, and brain activity in young children. But here’s the reality it missed: cash aid isn’t a lab experiment; it’s a lifeline meant to provide stability, safety, and dignity in the face of economic hardship.

The Measure of a Just Society

Cash is how people survive in a capitalist economy. It keeps the lights on, the rent paid, and food on the table. And when families have enough to meet their immediate needs, they don't just survive — they plan, adapt and thrive.

We’ve seen it ourselves. In our Youth Cash Transfer Program in East Palo Alto, unconditional monthly payments helped high school students cover essentials like food and transportation, while also investing in their education and family well-being. Mental health improved, financial skills strengthened, and students developed the agency to set and reach bigger goals.

In our Uplifting Immigrant Survivors Pilot, direct cash assistance gave survivors of gender-based violence the breathing room to focus on safety, healing, and securing stable housing. One participant told us it gave them “the space to breathe.”

Our experience isn’t unique. The results from hundreds of guaranteed income pilots nationwide and the expanded Child Tax Credit affirm a simple truth: when people have access to cash, they are better able to meet their needs, avoid debt, and improve their health, stability and financial well-being. The freedom and flexibility cash provides isn’t a side benefit. It’s the point.

View this on Substack

What the Study Really Tells Us

The Baby’s First Years study offers valuable insights into the limits of a single-variable intervention and the importance of context. The study ran during the COVID-19 pandemic, a time when both the treatment and control groups received unprecedented government support like stimulus checks and expanded unemployment benefits. That unique backdrop makes it difficult to isolate the effect of cash payments alone. It's a powerful reminder that a program’s impact can be muted or amplified by the world around it.

The amount matters, too. For families living on the edge, the $333 monthly payments were a lifeline — enough to prevent an eviction or keep food on the table. But the amount was far from what's needed to lift a family out of poverty or allow parents to consistently invest in opportunities that shape a child’s longer-term trajectory. That’s not a failure of cash aid. It’s a reflection of underinvestment. We’ve seen that when the investment matches the need, the impacts expand dramatically: families save more, avoid debt, improve their health, and create greater stability for their children.

Ultimately, the Baby’s First Years results reflect the study’s design and its narrow focus on a handful of developmental metrics, not a verdict on the power of cash itself. Even the researchers acknowledge this.

The important conversation isn’t whether cash “works” by a limited set of measures; it’s about why we should provide it in the first place: cash is one of the most efficient, effective, and dignified ways to ensure families can meet their needs, seize opportunities, and plan for the future. Providing that foundation is how we build a stronger, more just society.

Why This Matters Now More Than Ever

Without stability, opportunity is out of reach. But with enough money to meet their basic needs and plan for the future, families can move from a constant state of crisis to one of security, creating the conditions to improve their health, build financial strength and pursue their goals with confidence.

The lesson from Baby’s First Years isn’t to question cash: it’s to design it well. Amount matters. Timing matters. Pairing cash with services and systemic reform matters. A floor set too low won’t stop the flood, but that’s no argument against having a floor.

And as cuts to safety net programs like SNAP, TANF, and the Child Tax Credit push families to the brink, cash will matter more than ever. When other lifelines are stripped away, direct income becomes the anchor that prevents families from being swept into crisis.

We don’t measure the value of a healthy meal by whether it improves a child’s vocabulary. While well-fed children are better able to concentrate and learn, nourishment is essential in its own right. Cash is no different. It’s not a perk. It’s a basic need in our modern economy. Expanding access to it is not an experiment in generosity; it's the work of any society that calls itself just.

posts.title: Draining Vulnerable Communities to Feed the AI Race
posts.subtitle: The Intersection of Digital Transformation and Environmental Justice
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: The Intersection of Digital Transformation and Environmental Justice
posts.html:
While families in drought-stricken Texas are asked to ration water, a new wave of AI supercomputers is draining millions of gallons a day. This includes OpenAI’s massive “Stargate” campus near Abilene—a joint venture with Oracle and SoftBank—and Microsoft’s Azure facilities in Central Texas. The burden falls disproportionately on low-income, Black, and Brown communities already living with rising asthma rates, contaminated air, and unreliable utilities. These communities are being asked to sacrifice again for the so-called future of innovation.

Tech giants like Google, Meta, Apple, and OpenAI are leading the AI race, but with this new wave of technology, Silicon Valley’s biggest exports won’t just be technology and innovation—they will also be environmental and human harm. At mBOLDen Change, we believe progress should lift people up, not leave them behind. As AI reshapes our economy, education systems, and access to opportunity, we’re paying close attention to the human toll—a toll that isn’t shared equally. The same communities already facing disinvestment, environmental injustice, and poor health outcomes are being asked to shoulder the hidden costs of technological advancement.

This is the second in our series exploring how unchecked AI expansion threatens vulnerable communities. Today, we turn our focus to the environmental cost of the AI race—and who’s paying the price.

Winning the AI Race: A New Golden Age?

President Trump’s “Winning the Race: America’s AI Action Plan” is based on scaling back or eliminating regulations to establish the U.S. as a global leader in the technology. The plan’s introduction states:

“The United States is in a race to achieve global dominance in artificial intelligence (AI). Whoever has the largest AI ecosystem will set global AI standards and reap broad economic and military benefits… Winning the AI race will usher in a new golden age of human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security for the American people.

We need to build and maintain vast AI infrastructure and the energy to power it. To do that, we will continue to reject radical climate dogma and bureaucratic red tape, as the Administration has done since Inauguration Day. Simply put, we need to ‘Build, Baby Build!’”

But, at what price?

AI already permeates our daily lives. It’s the GPS in our cars, the Ring doorbell, your playlists, the list goes on and on. Most of us can agree that convenience should never come at the cost of public health or the basic human rights to clean air and water.

Yet the current push to “win” the AI race isn’t about playlists or efficiency. It’s about enabling government agencies and private corporations to train models, simulate war games, and predict human behavior. It’s about supercomputers capable of performing a quintillion operations per second, running 24/7—draining the earth’s resources and jeopardizing public health. This isn’t just technological intensity: it’s capitalism at its most extractive.

To meet these demands, environmental regulations on data centers are being discarded. Not only is the planet being drained of critical resources behind closed doors, but entire communities—especially those already burdened by health inequities and economic instability—are being pushed closer to the edge.

AI is quietly becoming one of the most energy-hungry, resource-draining systems on the planet, with a massive environmental cost. To win the AI race, we must burn more fossil fuels, extract increasing amounts of lithium and rare earth metals, and hoard water—accelerating climate degradation in the name of innovation and American dominance.

Water, Power, and Public Health

To win the AI race, the data center industry and big tech firms are ramping up investments to construct the infrastructure needed to support deeper AI integration across every sector of society. The impact on affected communities? An afterthought.

Water has become as critical to running data centers as electricity. Enormous amounts of cold water must be pumped through pipes to cool the machines inside these centers so they can perform nonstop calculations.

Newsha Ajami, a hydrologist and Director of Urban Water Policy at Stanford, notes that data center companies often demand municipalities make as much water available as possible, leveraging the tax revenue they pay. Yet because electricity is costlier than water, companies often build facilities in regions with cheap power, even in drought-stricken areas. As Ajami put it: “Water is an afterthought. Someone will figure that out later.” But impacted communities can’t wait for someone to figure it out later.

Access to clean water and air is a basic human need.

In Texas, data centers are projected to consume 49 billion gallons of water in 2025, a number expected to rise to 399 billion gallons by 2030—nearly 7% of the state’s total projected water use. This is happening as some residents are urged to conserve water and face surcharges for high usage. Between 2023 and 2024 alone, data centers in Central Texas, including some run by Microsoft, used a combined 463 million gallons of water.

There are no regulations forcing AI companies to limit their water use. While tech giants profit, working-class families, small towns, and already stressed ecosystems are left to fend for themselves in an unregulated environment.

Besides draining resources, energy-hungry data centers generate increased fossil fuel pollution in the frontline communities where they are located. A recent study linked AI-related pollution between 2019 and 2023 to health costs of $17 billion to $29 billion, and to at least 1,100 premature deaths. Residents are suffering real consequences—higher rates of COPD, asthma, and other respiratory illnesses. Meanwhile, industry executives promote data centers as a benefit to local communities, touting job creation and infrastructure investment. But these promises are often a smokescreen for the public health fallout.

This isn’t a distant or abstract concern—it’s happening right now. As the advocacy group Perfect Union reports, Elon Musk’s massive xAI data center in Memphis is burning enough gas to power a small city—with no permits and no pollution controls. Residents say they can’t breathe and they’re getting sicker. The facility is part of the infrastructure powering xAI’s “Grok for Government,” recently adopted by the Department of Defense. Perfect Union’s reporting makes it clear: the so-called national interest in AI is coming at a direct human cost to communities already burdened by environmental injustice.

View this on Substack

The Ethical Cost and the Cycle of Poverty

The environmental burden of AI is an ethical one. The burden isn’t shared equally. Black communities are 75% more likely to live near polluting sites. The same pattern holds for the power plants that run data centers, where over 60% in one state are located in areas with an above-average share of Black residents.

This environmental injustice is part of a cycle of poverty. Those trapped in environmentally degraded neighborhoods often face impossible choices. High medical costs, lower-paying jobs tied to poor health outcomes, and a lack of relocation options perpetuate generational poverty. This isn’t an accident—it’s by design.

The lack of transparency from AI providers and regulators makes it nearly impossible for communities to make informed decisions or protect themselves. Stripping away regulations only makes things worse.

As we pursue AI innovation, we can’t afford to ignore its fallout, especially for the communities most at risk. Government must intervene to regulate tech companies and their massive supercomputers, ensuring they don't shape the narrative—or the future—without accountability.

Collectively, we must all imagine a different path. One where AI models are smaller and more efficient, used more responsibly, and developed by a larger, more accountable ecosystem—not just a handful of Silicon Valley firms.

It’s not enough for tech giants to promise a brighter future. We must center the needs and health of vulnerable communities—and the planet—before it’s too late.

We’re told the AI race is in the national interest—that it’s simply the cost of progress. But when corporations prosper while working families ration water, breathe toxic air, and suffer in silence, that’s not innovation.

That’s exploitation. That’s capitalism.

At mBOLDen Change, we’re committed to building a stronger, fairer, and more equal society. That means blocking the harms inflicted on marginalized communities by extractive systems—and building toward systemic equity, where innovation no longer comes at the expense of human well-being or environmental justice.

This article is part of our ongoing series on the impact of AI on vulnerable communities, nonprofit systems, and the future of equity. Read our first post, and stay tuned for what’s next.

posts.title: How a Society Abandons Its Promise to the Next Generation
posts.subtitle: SCOTUS, Head Start, and the Dismantling of Public Education
posts.author: Minh Ngo
posts.excerpt: SCOTUS, Head Start, and the Dismantling of Public Education
posts.html:
I’ve worked to protect education rights for more than two decades. I lead mBOLDen Change, a nonprofit dedicated to building a more equal society for children. And, I am the parent of a child with disabilities.
