Every year, my family fights for his IEP, for his inclusion, for the supports he needs to thrive and the education services he is legally entitled to.

We have not yet had to place a call to the Office for Civil Rights. But knowing it was there — that we could — was important. It was a safety net, a line of defense, a backstop for families like ours navigating systems that too often fail to serve every child.

Now, that and other protections for vulnerable students are being ripped away. And while my family has had the resources, language, and legal literacy to advocate for what we need, millions of others do not: families of undocumented children who are now being told their toddlers aren’t welcome in preschool; families in rural districts that depend on federal funding just to keep the lights on; families with limited English, limited income, and no map for navigating a system that’s being deliberately made more punishing, more confusing, and more unequal.

The Trump administration’s attack on education closes the circle of opportunity for generations of kids, from preschoolers to college students, and threatens the health, security, and future of our communities and our country.

Why This Moment Matters

The Trump administration isn’t just reshaping education; it is breaching the implied promise of a free, appropriate and accessible education in the United States that has existed for generations. A nation that once aspired to expand opportunity is now actively shrinking it.

But this future isn’t inevitable. We still have power — in our voices, our votes, our stories, and our solidarity — to defend education, protect vulnerable students, resist erasure, and reclaim the belief that every child deserves a future shaped by opportunity, not ideology. It starts by staying educated about what’s happening and refusing to be silent.

Education is on the line. Speak up. Show up. Stay informed.

This is how a society abandons its promise to the next generation — slowly, then all at once.

SCOTUS Greenlights a Destructive Agenda

Since America’s earliest days, public education has been our greatest equalizer: a driver of civic participation, social mobility, and both individual and community survival. For generations, both Democratic and Republican administrations have aspired to expand the circle of opportunity and prosperity through education. Until now.

We are witnessing, in real time, the Trump administration’s systematic dismantling of public education. What’s being sold as “efficiency” and “local control” is an assault on equity, an erasure of civil rights, and a deliberate effort to turn education — once the backbone of democracy — into a privilege reserved for the few.

And, on July 14, the Supreme Court quietly handed the Trump administration a massive win. In a shadow docket decision, the Court lifted a lower court’s block on mass layoffs at the Department of Education, allowing Secretary Linda McMahon to fire nearly 1,400 DOE staff.

No explanation. No written opinions. Just permission to gut an entire federal agency.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor warned in her dissent that:

“the Department is responsible for providing critical funding and services to millions of students and scores of schools across the country. Lifting the District Court’s injunction will unleash untold harm, delaying or denying educational opportunities and leaving students to suffer from discrimination, sexual assault, and other civil rights violations without the federal resources Congress intended. The majority apparently deems it more important to free the Government from paying employees it had no right to fire than to avert these very real harms . . . Equity does not support such an inequitable result.”

Cruel New Policy Sends Chilling Message to Immigrant Families

On July 10, the Trump administration reclassified Head Start—a federally funded preschool program serving children from low-income families—as a “federal public benefit.” The move effectively banned undocumented children from enrolling and required local programs to verify immigration status. For over 60 years, Head Start has prepared more than 40 million children for school by providing early learning, health, nutrition, and family services — regardless of immigration status. Now, an estimated 115,000 children — 16% of current enrollment — could be excluded. And, families are withdrawing out of fear and confusion, even when their children remain eligible.

“This decision undermines the fundamental commitment that the country has made to children and disregards decades of evidence that Head Start is essential to our collective future.”

—Yasmina Vinci, Executive Director, National Head Start Association

Escalating the Assault on Disability Rights

The disability community has faced an unrelenting barrage of setbacks under the Trump administration. Cuts, delays, and policy shifts are endangering hard-won rights and eroding the public systems that millions of students depend on.

In February 2025, the Department of Education slashed over $600 million in teacher training grants. These grants funded programs supporting diverse teacher recruiting, culturally competent teaching, and addressing systemic inequities like racism and ableism.

Adult learners with disabilities were also sidelined when $715 million in adult basic education and literacy programs were part of the funds initially withheld by the Trump administration. This funding is crucial for adults seeking to complete high school, learn English, or improve literacy skills, and the delay caused significant disruption for programs that serve a large number of individuals with learning disabilities.

And the administration’s FY 2026 budget proposal goes even further, calling for a $4.5 billion cut to K–12 programs and the elimination of the University Centers for Excellence in Developmental Disabilities (UCEDDs). These centers — mandated by law in every state and territory — provided essential services to over 1.3 million individuals last year, including early intervention for children, training for disability support professionals, and self-advocacy education for youth and adults.

Meanwhile, restructuring plans have raised red flags around IDEA. While base funding for the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act has not been formally cut in the FY26 budget proposal, the administration’s plan to consolidate several IDEA programs into a single block grant and shift administration could reduce accountability and weaken enforcement, especially if oversight functions are moved out of the DOE. This proposed change would affect Parent Training and Information Centers, technical assistance, and training for special educators, among others.

And with the push toward privatization, students with disabilities face additional barriers. Voucher programs promoted in the administration’s platform divert public dollars to private schools that are not required to follow IDEA. That means fewer accommodations, fewer rights, and fewer guarantees for disabled students.

These aren’t just administrative tweaks. They’re systemic erosions — each one pushing disabled students and their families closer to the margins.

Civil Rights Enforcement Gutted

The DOE’s Office for Civil Rights (OCR) has been the frontline defender of educational equity. It investigates complaints of discrimination, enforces federal civil rights laws like Title VI (race), Title IX (sex, including gender identity and sexual orientation), and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (disability), and ensures that all students have equal access to education regardless of their background. Its work has been crucial in addressing issues from racial segregation and disproportionate discipline to sexual harassment and adequate services for students with disabilities.

Now, that critical work is being systematically dismantled. Seven of the DOE’s twelve regional Offices for Civil Rights have been shuttered, and their staff reassigned. This drastic action directly cripples the DOE’s ability to investigate and resolve complaints of discrimination, leaving fewer personnel and resources to handle a steady, often rising, caseload.

What does this mean in practice? Cases alleging discrimination based on race, sex, or disability will stall, languish, or simply go unaddressed. Schools facing complaints of racial bias in discipline, inaccessible facilities for students with disabilities, or unchecked sexual harassment, will feel emboldened to ignore inequities without the looming threat of federal investigation or enforcement.

This rollback disproportionately harms the nation’s most vulnerable young people — children of color, economically disadvantaged students, LGBTQ+ youth, and students with disabilities.

“This attack on education, K-12 and higher education, is about deliberately reinforcing racism and sexism, ableism, nativism, classism, so that people who are in marginalized communities or who just want a fair shot at the American Dream have those protections and opportunities stripped from them . . .”

— Andrea Abrams, Executive Director of the Defending American Values Coalition

Title I in Jeopardy: Undermining Opportunity

Title I of the Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) is the largest federal program supporting K-12 education, providing critical funding to schools with high numbers of low-income students. For decades, it has been a cornerstone of efforts to close achievement gaps and ensure every child, regardless of their zip code, has access to a quality education.

While the Trump administration’s FY 2026 budget proposal initially appears to hold core Title I-A funding for local educational agencies at approximately $18.4 billion, this headline number conceals significant cuts and radical restructuring. The budget proposal eliminates roughly $700 million in targeted Title I sub-programs, including:

  • $428 million cut to education supports for migrant students. This program provides essential services like academic tutoring, health screenings, and after-school programs for children of migrant agricultural workers—a population already facing significant educational instability.

  • $194 million cut to Comprehensive Literacy Development Grants.

  • $30 million cut to Innovative Approaches to Literacy.

  • $49 million cut to Support for Neglected and Delinquent Students.

But the bigger shift is structural. The administration proposes consolidating 18 existing K–12 formula and competitive grant programs, including Title I, into a single $2 billion grant. This aligns with Project 2025’s vision: block grants with no federal oversight or accountability.

The budget also eliminates the $890 million Title III program supporting English learners and immigrant students, and absorbs McKinney-Vento funding for homeless students into an underfunded block grant, diluting key protections in the process.

Financial Aid in Chaos: Undermining Access to Higher Education

The Department of Education's Office of Federal Student Aid (FSA) is the gateway to higher education for millions, overseeing a $1.7 trillion student loan portfolio and administering Pell Grants, which help over 30% of U.S. college students pay for tuition. This crucial agency manages the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA), disburses Pell Grants, oversees federal student loans, and administers vital programs like Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) and Income-Driven Repayment (IDR) plans.

However, the administration's sweeping layoffs have significantly impacted FSA, with hundreds of employees in the office laid off, amounting to nearly a quarter of its workforce. This drastic reduction is already creating chaos across the financial aid system: FAFSA processing delays, disruptions to the oversight and administration of student loans, reduced support for student borrowers.

These disruptions disproportionately impact first-generation students, low-income students, and students of color, who rely most heavily on federal financial aid to access and complete higher education.

Looking ahead, Project 2025 signals an even more drastic assault on federal student aid. Its blueprint proposes to fundamentally dismantle the federal government's role in making higher education affordable and accessible, pushing the financial burden onto individuals and potentially denying millions the opportunity to pursue postsecondary education or existing debt.

National Data Silenced: Blindfolding Policy and Perpetuating Disparity

The Institute of Education Sciences (IES) and its core statistical arm, the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), are the nation’s nonpartisan, independent authorities on education research, evaluation, and data. Since 1867, NCES has been mandated by Congress to collect, analyze, and report comprehensive statistics on the condition of American education, from early childhood through postsecondary. This includes tracking student performance, educational attainment, teacher and principal development, and disparities in achievement and resources across demographics. Their crucial work provides the objective data necessary for evidence-based policymaking, informing decisions at federal, state, and local levels, and enabling researchers, journalists, and the public to understand educational trends.

However, the administration’s budget cuts represent what education policy experts call "an assault on the nation’s education data infrastructure." The FY 2026 budget calls for slashing IES funding by a staggering 67%. This devastating cut would eliminate critical functions and open gaps in our ability to track equity and identify disparities. Without reliable, comprehensive national data, it becomes significantly harder to identify trends and disparities, evaluate program effectiveness, and ensure accountability and inform evidence-based policy.

“Just Return It to the States” Isn’t the Answer

Trump officials and their allies argue that education isn’t being eliminated, just returned to the states.

But, in the absence of federal oversight, local control has too often meant unequal funding, entrenched segregation, and unchecked discrimination. It was the federal government—not the states—that desegregated schools, mandated services for students with disabilities, English learners, and low‑income families. And it is (strike that — was) the Department of Education that enforces civil rights protections when schools fail to serve all children equitably.

Without that oversight, we’re left with a patchwork system, where a child’s opportunity depends on their ZIP code, immigration status, or ability to navigate a complex system.

On paper, local control sounds empowering. In practice, it reinforces the status quo— rewarding wealthy districts while under-resourcing those serving the most vulnerable. And without a federal commitment to equity, education itself becomes yet another tool of exclusion.

posts.title: There is No Justice. There is JUST US.
posts.subtitle: How Cash Programs Can Help Communities Weather the Trump Storm.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: How Cash Programs Can Help Communities Weather the Trump Storm.
posts.html:
There’s a saying we hear more and more these days:

“There is no justice. There is just us.”

For millions of households navigating rising costs, shrinking safety nets, and political cruelty disguised as fiscal policy, this statement isn’t just a slogan—it’s a gutting reality.

Donald Trump’s so-called “Big Beautiful Bill” offers yet another confirmation. Marketed as a pathway to prosperity, it’s actually a calculated blueprint for widening inequality:

  • Massive tax breaks for the wealthy.

  • Brutal cuts to food, healthcare, and basic cash supports for those who need them most.

  • A cruel indifference to children living in poverty, particularly in immigrant and Black and Brown communities.

The federal government should be a safety net, not a snare: a source of care and protection in hard times.

Instead, the Trump administration is doing the opposite, dismantling support systems and punishing those who need help most.

So what now?

Yes, we organize. We vote. We hold our elected officials accountable.

But families are slipping through the cracks right now.

And they cannot wait for D.C. to remember its duty to the people.

This is economic violence masquerading as a budget.

Tax Cuts for the Top 0.1%

Trump’s bill locks in and expands tax breaks that overwhelmingly benefit the wealthiest Americans and largest corporations. The top 0.1% stand to gain an average of over $300,000 per year, while the lowest-income families see net losses after factoring in benefit cuts.

A Gutted Child Tax Credit

The Child Tax Credit (CTC) should be one of our strongest tools to fight child poverty. Instead, the bill harms mixed-status families, blocking millions of U.S. citizen children from access. It also maintains income thresholds and refundability caps that ensure the poorest families receive the least support.

SNAP Cuts: Less Food, More Barriers

With $185 billion in cuts over ten years, the bill guts food assistance through expanded work requirements, cost shifts to states, and a freeze on benefit adjustments. More than 2 million people—including older adults, veterans, and working parents—could lose access.

Healthcare Cuts That Hurt the Most Vulnerable

The budget bill slashes over $1 trillion from Medicaid and CHIP by 2034, potentially stripping coverage from up to 17 million people. Rural hospitals face mass closures. New red tape and work requirements will push even eligible families off the rolls.

The Bottom Line

This bill is a top-down wealth grab sacrificing public health, food security, and childhood stability to further enrich the wealthy.

It accelerates the racial wealth gap and destabilizes the already-precarious lives of tens of millions.

What We Know Works: Cash

Cash transfers are one of the most effective poverty alleviation tools we have, helping to build a bridge to stability, economic security, better health outcomes, and social mobility.

What sets direct cash transfers and guaranteed income apart from other forms of economic assistance is their flexibility and inherent dignity. Whether it’s a one-time transfer or regular monthly payments, these approaches provide people with what they need without conditions, work requirements, restrictions, or bureaucratic hoops. Rooted in trust, they allow individuals to direct funds where they’re most needed, giving them the breathing room to stabilize, care for their families and invest in their futures. That could mean paying rent, seeking medical care, providing normalized experiences for their children, or saving for education and long-term goals.

As federal cuts take hold, direct cash transfers are a powerful tool that allows communities to respond in real time, empowering people to meet urgent needs, prevent displacement, and restore stability.

For states, municipalities and nonprofits facing rising need and shrinking federal support, cash transfer programs aren’t just a stopgap—they are a powerful way to meet the moment with dignity, speed, and impact.

At mBOLDen Change, we’ve been funding emergency cash transfers and guaranteed income since 2020. Our approach is simple: Give people what they need. Trust them to use it well. The impact speaks for itself.

We’ve seen:

  • Parents cover rent, groceries, medical care, and childcare.

  • Youth re-engage with school, build savings, and plan for their futures.

  • Immigrant survivors pay down debt, escape unsafe housing, and access care.

How Direct Cash Programs Can Help Communities Meet This Moment

From Stockton to Jackson, from Chicago to rural Georgia, communities across the country are turning to direct cash transfers and guaranteed income as a powerful response to the federal government’s systemic failure to care for its most vulnerable.

Nonprofits, local governments, private funders, and grassroots organizers are coming together to support these programs for pregnant people, youth aging out of foster care, immigrant families, low-wage workers, and others pushed to the margins. Together, they’re meeting this moment head-on and proving what’s possible when communities take the reins and trust people with the resources to care for themselves.

This is community care.

This is harm reduction.

This is infrastructure we can build—right now.

The fight for justice won’t be won solely at the voting booth or in the halls of Congress.

Across the country, it’s being forged now: in neighborhood clinics, in mutual aid circles, in cash pilots, in family kitchens, and among friends, neighbors and colleagues who refuse to look away.

  • Fund cash work. Prioritize those led by impacted communities.

  • Correct the myths. Share stories. Share data. Disrupt stigma.

  • Push for policy rooted in community. Economic security and human dignity should be a right.

  • Make Your Voice Heard. In community spaces. At marches. In letters to your elected officials. At the polls.

    “There is no justice.

    There is just us.

    All things that are are ours.

    But we must care.

    For if we do not care,

    We do not exist.”

    —Terry Pratchett

Let’s Set the Record Straight on Guaranteed Income

Last week, federal agents stormed Glass House Farms—a large, licensed, tax-paying cannabis company in California—in military-style fashion, detaining nearly 100 farmworkers. One worker was killed. Others were injured. And within hours, President Trump trotted out a familiar narrative steeped in fear, misinformation and dehumanizing rhetoric.

This is not new. The Trump administration has long relied on a dangerous script: Immigrant workers are “criminals.” They’re “stealing American jobs.” The raids are “necessary to protect the economy.”

Let’s be unequivocally clear: This isn’t about public safety. It is about targeting the most vulnerable among us while shielding those who profit from their exploitation. It was economic violence disguised as law enforcement. A show of force, yes. But one orchestrated by a system doing exactly what it was built to do.

The Uncomfortable Truth About “American Jobs”

To understand who actually performs the most grueling labor in this country, we have to confront our own history.

The Bracero Program: Our First Codified Exploitation

From 1942 to 1964, the U.S. ran the Bracero Program: an agreement with Mexico that brought millions of Mexican men to the U.S. as agricultural contract laborers during WWII labor shortages. While the program promised humane treatment and protections against discrimination and poor wages, it delivered widespread abuse: low pay, squalid housing, and a total lack of labor protections. It cemented our reliance on cheap, disposable labor from the Global South.

View this on Substack

When the Bracero program ended—thanks to pressure from labor unions and civil rights activists like Cesar Chavez—American farmers claimed their crops would rot without foreign labor.

Enter the “A-TEAM” (No, not the TV show)

In 1965, the U.S. government launched a PR stunt: the “A-TEAM,” or Athletes in Temporary Employment as Agricultural Manpower, recruiting 20,000 high school boys to work the fields.

Despite 18,000 sign-ups, only 3,300 showed up. Most quit within days. Some went on strike. The conditions were so exploitative that even this federally orchestrated whitewashed replacement collapsed almost immediately.

As Randy Carter, a former A-TEAM participant, later reflected: “We know the work they do. And they do it all their lives, not just one summer for a couple of months. And they raise their families on it. Anyone ever talks bad on them, I always think, 'Keep talking, buddy, because I know what the real deal is.'"

Historian Lori A. Flores explains it more bluntly:

“These [high school students] had the words and whiteness to say what they were feeling and could act out in a way that Mexican-Americans who had been living this way for decades simply didn’t have the power or space for the American public to listen to them… [The A-TEAM] reveals a very important reality: It’s not about work ethic. It’s about the fact that this labor is not meant to be done under such bad conditions and bad wages.”

This is still true today. The jobs are backbreaking, and the wages are insufficient to attract domestic workers. Even President Trump, in a rare moment of truth on Truth Social, admitted that “our very aggressive policy on immigration is taking very good, long time workers away from [farmers and hospitality employers], with those jobs being almost impossible to replace.”

In fact, 59% of Trump supporters agree that undocumented immigrants largely fill jobs American citizens don’t want.

“I can confidently say that most farmers in the country either laughed out loud or were just deflated by those comments… It just shows how uninformed and out of touch some of these officials are with what food production looks like in this country.”

— Helen McGrath, Ventura County citrus and avocado farmer, on Secretary Brooke Rollins’ suggestion that Medicaid recipients should replace deported farmworkers

The issue isn’t that immigrants are “taking” jobs. The issue is a system that allows employers to exploit a vulnerable workforce with impunity. If American workers are being displaced, blame the system and the people doing the hiring—not the people doing the hoeing.

Rhetoric vs. Reality: Unmasking the Truth About Immigration Raids

Let’s dissect the administration’s lies, one by one.

⚠️ TRUMP CLAIMS: They’re going after criminals.

THE TRUTH: This is perhaps the most insidious lie of all.

According to ICE’s own data as of June 14, 2025, 65% of those detained had no criminal convictions. Over 93% had no violent offenses. And even among those with convictions, the majority were for minor infractions like immigration violations or traffic offenses.

ICE deliberately labels individuals with pending charges as “criminals” to inflate their numbers and fuel public fear.

A federal judge recently blocked ICE raids in Los Angeles and several other California counties, explicitly banning detentions based on “apparent race or ethnicity” or “speaking Spanish.” These raids aren’t about crime. They’re about race, fear, and control.

And here’s the real kicker: ICE is arresting people for doing work that Americans won’t do, for wages Americans won’t tolerate, under conditions no one should have to endure.

The real crimes are exploitation, wage theft, and labor trafficking.

And those crimes are being committed by employers—who almost never face consequences.

⚠️ TRUMP CLAIMS: Undocumented immigrants are a burden on taxpayers.

THE TRUTH: Another myth designed to stoke resentment.

Undocumented immigrants contribute billions in taxes annually despite being barred from most public benefits. In 2022, they paid an estimated $96.7 billion in federal, state, and local taxes, including nearly $20 billion in income tax and $32 billion in payroll tax.

In 40 out of 50 states, undocumented immigrants pay a higher effective tax rate than the top 1%.

Meanwhile, billionaires and corporations enjoy tax cuts, subsidies, and special treatment.

So if you’re looking for freeloaders: look up, not down.

⚠️ TRUMP CLAIMS: This is about restoring order.

THE TRUTH: What he really means is restoring control over labor and dictating who gets to live and work with dignity.

These raids are a show of force. They are designed to intimidate, to create fear, to silence workers, and to send a message that immigrant workers lack fundamental rights and safety.

ICE isn’t being deployed to protect communities. It’s being used as a tool of economic and social repression.

🔍 THE PUBLIC DOESN’T WANT THIS

Crucially, recent public opinion data directly contradicts the idea that aggressive enforcement reflects a public mandate.

A Gallup poll released in July 2025 reveals a significant shift in American attitudes towards immigration:

  • The percentage of Americans who want less immigration dropped from 55% in 2024 to just 30%, returning to 2021 levels.

  • A record-high 79% of U.S. adults now say immigration is good for the country, up from 64% last year. This positive shift spans all major political parties.

  • Support for punitive measures is fading: backing for increased Border Patrol agents has fallen by 17 points (now at 59%), and support for expanding the U.S.-Mexico border wall has dropped by 8 points (now at 45%).

  • Meanwhile, 78% now support a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants—up from 70% last year.

Bottom line: The public is not calling for more raids.

The current enforcement approach is not only cruel, it’s increasingly out of step with the values and views of the country it claims to protect.

The System is Working Exactly as Designed

ICE didn’t raid a boardroom. They raided a farm. They didn’t detain the CEO. They detained the workers picking crops.

This is not a bug in the system. It’s the point of the system:

To criminalize survival.

To protect capital.

To sacrifice workers to preserve wealth.

Employer Accountability: The Enforcement Gap

U.S. law is clear: under the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, employers who knowingly hire undocumented workers face severe penalties, including fines, asset forfeiture, even prison.

And yet, ICE overwhelmingly targets workers, not employers. There is a notable absence of public data on employer prosecutions or penalties. While there are occasional high-profile cases, they are the exception, not the rule.

Programs like IMAGE (Mutual Agreement between Government and Employers) even let employers voluntarily hand over records to reduce their fines.

When employers face minimal risk, there's little economic incentive to ensure a fully legal workforce, perpetuating reliance on undocumented labor and providing a continuous pool of individuals for ICE to target. If this were really about jobs or national security, we’d be targeting those writing the paychecks, not those cashing them.

Why the “Legal Pathways” Argument Doesn’t Hold

Yes, we have visa programs like H-2A and H-2B. But they’re expensive, complicated, and inefficient.

Employers must pay high fees, navigate multiple federal agencies, and comply with complex rules. Only 80% of certified H-2A jobs result in actual visa issuance.

The government's failure to provide adequate, accessible, and comprehensive legal pathways for temporary labor directly contributes to the presence of undocumented workers. This means that the "problem" ICE is tasked with addressing is, in part, a consequence of an inadequate legal immigration system. The raids, therefore, become a punitive response to a systemic issue that policy itself helps to create, rather than a solution to the underlying labor needs.

For many employers, the calculation is simple: it’s easier and cheaper to hire undocumented workers since they risk no real penalty.

The system incentivizes exploitation and then punishes the workers it pushes into the margins.

What We Need: Systemic Equity, Not Political Theater

At mBOLDen Change, we believe that Safety, dignity, and economic security are basic and universal rights, not privileges. We are committed to building a society where:

  • No worker is arrested for trying to survive.

  • Exploitative employers are held legally accountable.

  • Labor protections apply to all workers, regardless of status. We must recognize that cheap labor—born from exploitative conditions—ultimately harms everyone. It not only suppresses wages and diminishes the dignity of work for laborers but also erodes our collective values, suggesting that human exploitation is an acceptable cost of doing business. A truly equitable system values all people and their labor, ensuring fair wages, safe conditions, and humane treatment, without distinction of origin or status.

This requires a complete shift from a punitive, fear-based immigration model to a rational, just, and humane system.

That Means PolicyMakers Must:

  • Reform visa programs and expand legal pathways like H-2A and H-2B so they are functional, accessible, and free from abuse.

  • Pass the Farm Workforce Modernization Act, which offers a pathway to legal status and helps stabilize the essential agricultural workforce.

  • Enforce employer accountability and end the era of impunity for corporate violators who knowingly exploit unauthorized labor.

  • Center human dignity in every policy decision, from labor standards to enforcement protocols.

  • Address the root causes that drive migration in the first place, including economic dislocation, climate disruption, and our own foreign policy failures.

Every human being deserves to live in safety, freedom, and dignity. This is not a radical idea. It’s a moral imperative.

posts.title: Medicaid: A Safety Net by Many Names
posts.subtitle: Millions are about to lose health coverage under a new federal law and too many don't even know it. Here’s how to know if you’re at risk, and what to do next.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: Millions are about to lose health coverage under a new federal law and too many don't even know it. Here’s how to know if you’re at risk, and what to do next.
posts.html:
Budgets are Moral Documents. This One Cuts Deep.

Access to affordable healthcare is a lifeline. But this July 4, President Trump signed a devastating federal budget into law, setting off a wave of rollbacks that will gut the nation’s most vital public health coverage: Medicaid.

According to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO), nearly 12 million more Americans are expected to be uninsured by 2034 due to cuts in federal Medicaid funding and reduced support for ACA marketplace subsidies. Many of those affected may not even realize they’re at risk because their health plan doesn’t go by the name “Medicaid.” (NPR)

Millions Don’t Realize They Are Medicaid Recipients

Medicaid is the country’s largest public health insurance program, serving children, seniors, pregnant people, low-income families and individuals with disabilities. But it doesn’t always go by that name. Because it’s a joint federal and state program, states have flexibility to rebrand Medicaid with names meant to sound more local or more like private insurance.

That flexibility has a cost: millions of people don’t realize they’re Medicaid recipients.

If you are covered by any of these Medicaid programs, your healthcare is on the line:

  • Alabama: Alabama Medicaid

  • Alaska: DenaliCare

  • Arizona: AHCCCS (Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System)

  • Arkansas: ARHOME; Arkansas Medicaid

  • California: Medi-Cal

  • Colorado: Health First Colorado

  • Connecticut: HUSKY Health (A–D)

  • Delaware: Diamond State Health Plan

  • District of Columbia: DC Healthy Families

  • Florida: Florida Medicaid; SMMC (Statewide Medicaid Managed Care)

  • Georgia: Georgia Families

  • Hawaii: Med-QUEST

  • Idaho: Idaho Medicaid

  • Illinois: Illinois Medicaid / All Kids

  • Indiana: HIP; Hoosier Healthwise; Hoosier Care Connect; M.E.D. Works

  • Iowa: IA Health Link

  • Kansas: KanCare

  • Kentucky: Kentucky Medicaid

  • Louisiana: Healthy Louisiana

  • Maine: MaineCare

  • Maryland: HealthChoice

  • Massachusetts: MassHealth

  • Michigan: Michigan Medicaid

  • Minnesota: Medical Assistance

  • Mississippi: MississippiCAN

  • Missouri: MO HealthNet

  • Montana: Montana Medicaid

  • Nebraska: Nebraska Medicaid; ACCESSNebraska

  • Nevada: Nevada Medicaid

  • New Hampshire: NH Medicaid

  • New Jersey: NJ FamilyCare

  • New Mexico: Centennial Care

  • New York: New York State Medicaid

  • North Carolina: NC Medicaid

  • North Dakota: North Dakota Medicaid

  • Ohio: Ohio Medicaid

  • Oklahoma: SoonerCare

  • Oregon: Oregon Health Plan (OHP)

  • Pennsylvania: Medical Assistance

  • Rhode Island: RIte Care

  • South Carolina: Healthy Connections Medicaid

  • South Dakota: South Dakota Medicaid

  • Tennessee: TennCare

  • Texas: Texas Medicaid (STAR; STAR+PLUS)

  • Utah: Utah Medicaid

  • Vermont: Vermont Medicaid; Green Mountain Care

  • Virginia: Cardinal Care

  • Washington: Apple Health

  • West Virginia: West Virginia Medicaid

  • Wisconsin: BadgerCare Plus; ForwardHealth

  • Wyoming: Wyoming Medicaid

What the New Law Does

The new law puts an entire safety net in jeopardy. Here’s what’s changing and why it matters:

Nearly 12 million projected to lose coverage: According to the Congressional Budget Office, reductions in federal Medicaid and ACA marketplace funding will leave almost 12 million more Americans uninsured by 2034. This includes millions pushed out of coverage due to administrative barriers, lost subsidies, and tighter eligibility. (Congress.gov)

  • Mandatory Work Requirements: Beginning in 2027, most Medicaid expansion recipients will need to prove work or community engagement. Even if you’re working, reporting errors or red tape could result in termination.

  • Frequent Eligibility Checks: More paperwork, more often. States will be required to redetermine eligibility every 6 months or more, increasing the risk of people falling through the cracks.

  • Federal Funding Cuts: Deep cuts in federal support will push states to limit services, reduce benefits, or make eligibility rules even more restrictive.

  • Cost Sharing: Starting in 2028, expansion populations will face mandatory co-pays of up to $35 per visit. That turns a routine doctor’s visit into a financial burden.

  • Exclusions for Non-Citizens: Fewer immigrants and mixed-status families will qualify, even if they’re lawfully present.

Cutting medicaid access shrinks the safety net and makes healthcare harder to access for those who need it most.

Policies and budgets reflect what we value as a society. And, this new law sends a message that some lives, some families, and some communities matter less.

And the consequences are severe:

  • Children lose access to preventative care like well visits, immunizations, and dental screenings. A study found that children enrolled in Medicaid were more likely to get preventive care but those odds increased dramatically when parents also had Medicaid. Well-child visit rates jumped from 29% (uninsured) to 43% (child-only coverage), and to 67% when both parent and child were enrolled, showing that family coverage is essential to children’s health outcomes. (PMC)

  • Pregnant people may be cut off from prenatal and postpartum care, increasing risks for maternal and infant mortality. Medicaid finances 41% of U.S. births. (KFF)

  • Seniors and individuals with disabilities can lose home- and community-based services, pushing them into institutional settings or leaving them without care altogether. Nearly 5.6 million people rely on Medicaid for Long-term Services and Supports. (KFF)

  • Low-income adults may suffer severe consequences, including delays in care and even increased mortality: new modeling predicts that reductions in Medicaid access could lead to nearly 15,000 additional deaths per year among adults aged 25–64, alongside skipped treatments, financial hardship, and worsening chronic disease outcomes. (Keck School of Medicine of USC)

We must stop treating Medicaid like a line item and start seeing it for what it is: vital social infrastructure. It safeguards health, empowers families and helps build stronger, more resilient communities.

View this on Substack

What You Should Do If You Are on Medicaid

  • Know Your Plan: Look at your insurance card. If your coverage is on the list above, this law may affect you.

  • Monitor Communications: Medicaid paperwork is real and missing a form can mean losing your coverage.

  • Stay Informed: Follow reputable news sources and healthcare advocacy organizations for updates on how these changes are being implemented in your state. Here are a few of our recommendations:

    • KFF Medicaid Tracker — Offers in-depth, nonpartisan analysis and state-level data on Medicaid enrollment, policy changes, and spending.

    • Families USA — A leading national health advocacy group with action alerts, toolkits, and news on healthcare justice.

    • National Health Law Program (NHeLP) — Legal advocacy to protect Medicaid access, especially for underserved communities.

  • Speak Up: While the bill has been signed into law, its implementation is ongoing. Share your concerns with your state legislators and officials and continue to engage with advocacy groups.

    • Use tools like OpenStates.org to find and contact your representatives. Your personal story about how Medicaid (by whatever name it's called in your state) impacts you and your family is powerful.

  • Spread the Word: Many people don’t know they’re on Medicaid. Forward this, post it, talk about it. Awareness is a form of resistance.

Healthcare is a human right.

Your health, and the health of your community, depends on understanding and preparing for these changes. Don’t let your care — or your neighbor’s — be dismantled without a fight.

But you don’t need to be a billion‑dollar organization to stand up for your people. With immigration enforcement ramping up in many parts of the country, employers are facing new pressures—and new responsibilities. Now more than ever, workers and families need protection. And employers need clear, practical ways to go beyond the minimum and show up with courage and care.

At mBOLDen Change, we believe that creating a just workplace isn’t just about legal checklists—it’s about leadership that builds trust, promotes fairness, and fosters a workplace where everyone feels safe and supported.

That’s why we created this resource for employers:

[🔗 Download the Toolkit on Our Website]

This isn’t just about policies. It’s about people. About taking tangible steps to ensure immigrant workers—and their families—feel safe, valued, and protected, especially in times of heightened enforcement and fear.

Why This Matters

First and foremost, immigrant workers are human beings—with rights, dignity, and inherent worth. As workers and as a workforce, they are essential to our economy, our communities, and our shared livelihoods.

And yet, they are too often left vulnerable.

Many employers want to support their workers but don’t always know where to start. This Toolkit was created for them.

Whether you implement one policy or many, every step you take helps build a workplace rooted in safety, trust, and fairness.

posts.title: Baby Bonds Were Meant to Close the Wealth Gap. 'Trump Accounts’ Are a Reverse Robin Hood.
posts.subtitle: As states advance real equity solutions, Trump distorts the purpose of baby bonds.
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: As states advance real equity solutions, Trump distorts the purpose of baby bonds.
posts.html:
We’ve been exploring baby bonds for years.

As a policy idea, baby bonds caught our attention because they go to the root of America’s generational (read: racial) wealth gap.

So, when we saw the recent headlines about Trump’s proposal for $1,000 accounts for babies born during his presidency, we gasped. Given his track record of co-opting and distorting progressive ideas, we had a feeling his proposal would warp the concept beyond recognition—and it did.

What are Baby Bonds?

The idea of giving babies a financial start in life isn’t new. For decades, policymakers, academics, and advocates have floated ideas like publicly funded trust funds or child savings accounts, often tied to education.

But in recent years, baby bonds have come to represent a comprehensive, justice-oriented policy framework focused on closing the wealth gap. As envisioned by economists Darrick Hamilton and William Darity, the model includes these key components:

“An economic birthright to capital.” — Darrick Hamilton

  1. Universal eligibility – All children would be automatically enrolled at birth

  2. Financially progressive – Children from lower-wealth households would receive progressively larger deposits

  3. Public funding – Baby bonds would be financed by government and not impact household eligibility for public benefits

  4. Substantial endowment – Each account would be designed to grow into a meaningful sum by adulthood, using investments that protect the principal and generate returns to support major wealth-building opportunities

  5. Flexible use of funds – Funds could be used for a range of wealth-building activities like home ownership, higher education, or entrepreneurship

  6. Individual recipient – The young person, not their parents or the state, is the account beneficiary and decision maker about how the funds are used

View this on Substack

📍Current State Models

Connecticut Baby Bonds
Connecticut was the first state to pass baby bonds legislation in 2021. Under this program, $3,200 is invested by the state on behalf of each baby whose birth is covered by HUSKY Health (Connecticut’s Medicaid program). The funds are professionally managed and are projected to grow to between $11,000 and $24,000 by the time the child reaches adulthood.

Eligible uses include:

  • Buying a home in Connecticut

  • Starting or investing in a business

  • Higher education or job training

  • Retirement savings

📄 Learn more: CT Baby Bonds – Office of the Treasurer

California HOPE Accounts
California launched the HOPE (Hope, Opportunity, Perseverance, and Empowerment) for Children Trust Account program in 2022 to address intergenerational poverty.

It provides support to children in long-term foster care or those who lost a parent or caregiver to COVID-19. Each eligible child receives a state-funded account expected to grow to approximately $4,500 by age 18.

While the dollar amounts are modest, the intent is clear: to offer children who’ve experienced systemic barriers a tangible on-ramp to wealth-building.

📄 Learn more: HOPE for Children – CA State Treasurer’s Office

🌱 Momentum Across the Country

In addition to these state models, other states, including New Mexico, Vermont, Rhode Island, and Washington State, have introduced legislation or pilots aimed at building baby bond infrastructure.

One of the most exciting pilots we’re watching is the Freedom Futures initiative from the GRO Fund in Georgia—a bold initiative that brings together two tools we believe deeply in: guaranteed income and baby bonds.

Freedom Futures: Cash for Today, Capital for Tomorrow Baby Bonds Pilot Program

Freedom Futures is a four year pilot program that includes three key components:

  • An investable lump sum (“Baby Bond”)

  • $500/month guaranteed income

  • Financial advising services

The Baby Bond provides “seed capital” for wealth building strategies, while the guaranteed income offers unrestricted monthly cash to help recipients meet immediate needs. Together, they form an exciting two-pronged approach to stability and mobility.

The program is expected to launch in 2025 and is currently seeking partners and supporters.

👉 Click here to learn more or donate to this promising solution.

What Trump Is Proposing—and Why It Misses the Mark

Enter “Trump Accounts.” On the surface, they sound like baby bonds. But they miss the core intent and foundational principles.

Greg Leiserson, Senior Fellow at the Tax Law Center at NYU Law and former Deputy Assistant Secretary for Tax Analysis at the U.S. Treasury, says:

“Trump Accounts serve no clear purpose and would exclude vulnerable children.”

As Leiserson points out, the proposal would:

  • Exclude U.S. citizen children if their parents lack Social Security Numbers—even if the child has one

  • Exclude children of non-filers, including low-income families

  • Fail to coordinate with existing benefits or savings programs

  • Leave key administrative questions unanswered

He also notes a broader pattern:

“The proliferation of tax-preferred savings accounts for various purposes has created a menu of tax subsidies for people who already have spare time and money who can allocate their savings to these various accounts to maximize their tax benefits. They serve, generally, as a transfer of public resources to already well-off filers.”

These concerns are echoed in The New Yorker, where journalist John Cassidy writes in his weekly column, The Financial Page, that while Trump proposal may sound family-friendly, it is ultimately regressive in both design and effect:

“According to a report by the Congressional Budget Office, over all, the bill’s provisions, including the new accounts, would reduce the financial resources of households in the bottom tenth of the income distribution by about sixteen-hundred dollars a year relative to a baseline scenario, and raise the resources of households in the top tenth by an average of about twelve thousand dollars a year.”

"In other words, it’s a reverse-Robin Hood.”

Our Take

Let’s be honest: by the time Trump’s proposal makes it through the legislative process (if it does at all), it will likely be even further removed from anything resembling equity-driven policy. One thing is certain—it bears little to no resemblance to the baby bonds envisioned by Darrick Hamilton and William Darity.

Now is the time to clarify—not compromise—what a national baby bonds policy should strive for:

  • To close the racial wealth gap

  • To build generational opportunity

  • To offer all children, not just some, a fair start

Let’s keep pushing for the real thing.

📚 Want to learn more? Start here:

  • Tax Law Center – Trump Accounts Serve No Clear Purpose

  • The New Yorker – Trump’s Cash-for-Kids Savings Scheme

  • The State of Baby Bonds – Urban Institute (2023)

  • ACLU of WA – Baby Bonds: A Path Toward Prosperity

  • PBS – What Experts Think About the $1,000 Trump Accounts for Babies

Share if you believe baby bonds should be about equity—not branding.

posts.title: Public Education Should Be a Federally Protected Civil Right
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: Public education has long been a pillar of American society — but it has never been guaranteed as a federally protected right.
posts.html:
Public education has long been a pillar of American society — but it has never been guaranteed as a federally protected right.

In the 1973 case San Antonio Independent School District v. Rodriguez, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Constitution does not explicitly guarantee a right to education. While the 14th Amendment’s Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses provide some important safeguards, they have never been enough to ensure that every student receives a high-quality, equitable education.

That’s why the federal government has a critical role to play.

Why We Need a Federal Role in Education

In 1979, President Jimmy Carter established the U.S. Department of Education (DOE) to bring together fragmented federal education programs under one roof. His goal was ambitious: to ensure the federal government actively enforced civil rights laws, tackled systemic inequities, and guaranteed that all students — regardless of race, income, geography, or ability — had equal access to a quality education.

Since its founding, the Department of Education has played a vital role in protecting students’ civil rights, providing funding to underserved districts, supporting students with disabilities, and ensuring that states meet basic standards of equity and inclusion.

Now, that critical role is under attack.

The current administration is pushing to eliminate the Department of Education altogether, arguing that education should be returned fully to the states. They say it’s about reducing bureaucracy and restoring “local values.” But the truth is, it’s about weakening students’ civil rights and accountability while paving the way for privatization, school vouchers, and a patchwork system where access to a quality, equitable education depends entirely on a child’s zip code.

What’s at Stake Now

We’ve seen this before — and we still see it today. While the creation of the Department of Education helped reduce some of the most glaring disparities in access and funding, inequities persist. Black, brown, immigrant, rural, low-income students, and students with disabilities continue to face systemic barriers.

Without federal standards and oversight, who will fight for them? Who will hold states accountable? Dismantling the Department of Education would reverse hard-won progress and deepen inequities for students across the country.

The Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights (OCR) shows us why federal enforcement matters. Since its founding, OCR has protected students by collecting data on opportunity gaps, issuing civil rights guidance, and investigating discrimination.

  • In Cleveland, OCR found that Latinx students — 14% of the Cleveland Metropolitan School District’s population — were denied equitable access to STEM programs due to school placements and the lack of Spanish-language outreach.

  • In Henrico County, Virginia, OCR uncovered stark disparities in advanced coursework, graduation rates, and test performance between predominantly Black and white schools.

These are just two of thousands of investigations that have led to concrete changes — ensuring more equitable access to learning opportunities for millions of students.

As AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler warns:

“Shuttering the Department of Education is a radical plan, ripped from the pages of Project 2025, that will close the doors of opportunity for America’s students. Without the Department of Education, working people will have one more hurdle to access the financial aid they need to go to college or pursue a trade. Kids from working-class families — especially kids with disabilities — will be left behind, unable to access the education they need to succeed. States, cities, and towns will be forced to stretch their already tight budgets to cover the loss in federal funding, jeopardizing essential programs.”

What We Stand to Lose

Public education must be more than a patchwork of local policy decisions. It must be a civil right—one that is protected, resourced, and enforced at the federal level.

Eliminating the Department of Education would:

  • Deepen inequality across states and districts

  • Strip away critical civil rights protections

  • Undermine the federal commitment to students with disabilities, English learners, and low-income communities

  • Leave rural and underserved areas without the federal support they rely on

A country that enables educational inequity squanders the potential of millions of future workers, thinkers, dreamers, and leaders.

Public education is not a privilege. It’s a necessity.

It should reflect our highest values — not the lowest bar each state is willing to set.

It’s time we treat it like a federally protected civil right.

Take Action

📣 Submit a Public Comment by June 20

The U.S. Department of Education is collecting public comments on a major policy shift:

“Priorities, Requirements, Definitions, and Selection Criteria: Evidence-Based Literacy, Education Choice, and Returning Education to the States”

(Docket ID: ED–2025–OS–0020)

This proposed rule paves the way for dismantling the Department of Education, shifting responsibility to the states, and expanding privatization efforts through vouchers and charter programs. It directly threatens federal protections for students with disabilities, English learners, and those in low-income and rural communities.

Submit your public comment by June 20 to make your voice heard.

👉 Go to www.regulations.gov

👉 Search: ED-2025-OS-0020

👉 Click the title: Priorities, Requirements, Definitions, and Selection Criteria…

👉 Hit “Comment”

Tell the Department:

  • You OPPOSE dismantling the Department of Education

  • You SUPPORT protecting students’ civil rights and equitable access to opportunity

  • Returning education to the states — without federal accountability — is not reform. It’s regression.

🗳️ Contact Your Elected Officials

The President cannot eliminate the Department of Education without Congressional approval. That means your voice — and your vote — can help stop this.

Tell them: Protect public education and the civil rights of our students. Oppose efforts to dismantle the Department of Education.

Use this tool from Common Cause to call or email your representatives.

📧 Sample Message to Send

Subject: Defend Public Education and Civil Rights — Protect the Department of Education

Dear [Representative/Senator],

I am deeply concerned about efforts to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education. This proposal is not about streamlining government — it’s about walking away from our national commitment to educational equity.

The Department of Education plays a critical role in enforcing civil rights, supporting students with disabilities and English learners, and ensuring that schools serving low-income and rural communities receive the resources they need. Eliminating it would roll back decades of hard-won progress and harm millions of students.

Public education should reflect our highest values — not the lowest bar each state is willing to set. I urge you to stand firmly against any attempt to weaken or abolish the Department of Education. Our students — and our democracy — depend on it.

Sincerely,

posts.title: What does it mean to be human in the age of AI?
posts.author: Minh Ngo
posts.excerpt: So, what does it mean to be human in the age of AI?
posts.html:
So, what does it mean to be human in the age of AI?

What does real connection look like when the stories we hear (or the visuals we see) might be generated by a machine?

Are narratives just a collection of well-curated words strung together for maximum engagement? Or are they lived experiences, messy, emotional, flawed, beautiful, connecting people across difference and building trust in ways no algorithm ever could?

Because if we reach a point where we can’t tell the difference between a human voice and a synthetic one, where computer-generated empathy is indistinguishable from the real thing . . . where does that leave us?

And more importantly, who and what gets lost?

In 1710, Jonathan Swift wrote, “Falsehood flies, and the truth comes limping after it.” Two centuries later, Mark Twain echoed those words—but got all the credit. In today’s world of AI and social media, that quote wouldn’t just be misattributed: it would be optimized, monetized, deep-faked, turned into a meme, posted with a purchased or fake verified checkmark, and probably credited to someone with more followers.

Sure, this is a harmless example (and maybe not even a good one). But in the real world, AI-generated mis/disinformation has already fueled political violence, undermined public health campaigns, and targeted vulnerable communities with viral falsehoods. The consequences are not theoretical. It’s eroding social cohesion, impacting how we treat one another, threatening the ability of civil society and nonprofits to speak truth and build power, and undermining democracy.

That’s the speed and scale of disinformation in the age of AI. It’s not just that lies and falsehoods spread faster; they spread “smarter”—slipping past our defenses by mimicking authenticity, exploiting trust, and hijacking the very tools we once relied on to build shared understanding and emotional connection.

So where does that leave us? Especially those of us in the nonprofit world whose work and credibility often depends on public trust, human connection, and stories that move us.

Honestly? I don’t know. This question has been keeping me up at night in recent months.

But I do know that as nonprofits we should not fall into the familiar cycle of being late adopters of new technology. The opportunities that AI presents are too great to sit out. But most importantly, we should not just be users and consumers of this double-edged tech.

We must be at the forefront of the fight for guardrails and regulation to address the risks associated with algorithmic bias, discrimination, the erosion of privacy, the amplification of disinformation, the environmental devastation, and the threat AI poses to human creativity—especially the voices of artists, storytellers, and culture-shapers whose work risks being scraped, mimicked, or silenced.

These aren’t risks that are coming. They’re already here.

Sure, we could wax nostalgic for a world without AI, but let’s be real: that ship has sailed (and it’s already halfway to Mars on a SpaceX Starship). AI is here. It’s evolving fast. It’s everywhere. And it’s not going back in the box.

Just this week, The New York Times reported that OpenAI is rolling out “AI-native universities,” embedding ChatGPT into campus life—from customized study bots provided by professors to recruiter chatbots offered by career services, and more. California State University, with more than 460,000 students across 23 campuses, is already onboard to reshape how students learn and engage in real time using AI tools.

As AI becomes more embedded in how we learn, work, create and live, the need to counter its misuse, especially in the spread of disinformation, has never felt more urgent.

Last month, the researchers behind “Weaponized Storytelling: How AI Is Helping Researchers Sniff Out Disinformation Campaigns” made a compelling case: the same technology that’s fanning the flames of disinformation might also be one of our best tools for fighting it. Their work at Florida International University trains AI to understand narrative structures, trace personas and timelines, and decode cultural references—essentially using AI tools to “identify when a story doesn’t add up.” Sounds both wild and deeply necessary.

I don’t believe we can or should rely on AI alone to save us from itself.

At the end of the day, technology doesn’t replace trust. And algorithms, no matter how advanced, can’t stand in for accountability, critical thinking, or informed communities. In order to meet this moment with integrity, we need to demand:

• Regulation — real, enforceable policy that demands transparency from platforms and accountability from creators of generative AI.

• Media literacy — not just in schools, but in community centers, senior circles, faith gatherings, and those nonstop group chats where links fly before anyone checks them. It should live on social media too. We put warning labels on cigarettes and cleaning products. We should put them on the very platforms spreading viral disinformation. People need tools to decode what they’re seeing, hearing, and sharing.

• Treating information ecosystems like public infrastructure — not just profit streams for tech companies. Because when the pipelines of public discourse get polluted, it’s the communities we serve that get poisoned first.

So, back to where I started—what does it mean to be human in the age of AI?

Those of us doing social impact work know the power of authenticity. We’ve watched how a survivor sharing their truth can change policy. We’ve seen how an immigrant narrating their escape from oppression can shift what people believe is possible. We’ve experienced hearts open as a young person tells their story of struggle and empowerment.

That’s not just content. That’s connection.

So yes, AI might be able to connect the words into a story. But it can’t connect with the weight of it. Only we can.

And that’s the part we have to protect. Fiercely.

(And yes, I am still a human writing this. At least . . . until Morpheus shows up and offers me the red pill.)

posts.title: The System Does Not Support Environmental Justice
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: Access to a healthy environment and protection from disproportionate environmental burdens should be a baseline right of every U.S. resident.
posts.html:
Access to a healthy environment and protection from disproportionate environmental burdens should be a baseline right of every U.S. resident. So why isn’t it?

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) once defined environmental justice as the fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people regardless of race, color, national origin, or income, with respect to the development, implementation, and enforcement of environmental laws regulations, and policies.

Given this country’s history and the agency’s own track record, that sounds very aspirational.

Not surprisingly, the term “Environmental Justice” was recently removed from the EPA’s website.

On May 22,, 2025, House Republicans under pressure from the White House passed a sweeping spending plan. While ostensibly a budget and tax bill, it guts already inadequate environmental protections for air, land and water.

Dubbed the “Big Beautiful Bill,” the administration’s plan accelerates environmental rollbacks, slashes funding for disaster preparedness, and undermines community recovery. In short: it sacrifices the health, safety, and stability of low-income families to protect polluters and profits.

Injustice by Design.

Environmental injustice has always been by design. The people most burdened by pollution and climate-related harm are overwhelmingly Black, Brown, Indigenous, low-wealth, rural, immigrant, and refugee communities—groups historically excluded from political power and impacted by systemic racism.

From highways that produce toxic and hazardous waste to factories sited near their schools and homes, these communities weren’t protected from harm—they were targeted for it.

The consequences are well documented:

  • Air pollution fuels asthma, cancer, and developmental disorders in children.

  • Water contamination causes gastrointestinal illnesses, infections, respiratory issues, and more.

  • Environmental disasters—like wildfires, floods, and toxic spills—hit hardest where safety nets are weakest.

In America, environmental ambivalence is policy. For far too many, the risk of breathing, drinking, or living safely depends on your zip code.

Should our government protect the vulnerable—or continue to sacrifice them?

Environmental Justice for All.

Rooted in the civil rights movement and shaped by decades of community mobilization and grassroots resistance, today’s environmental justice movement continues to combat environmental racism and the systems that sustain it.

Fighting for environmental injustice is fighting for basic human rights, the safety and well-being of communities, and sustainable health equity.

To achieve this, we need policies that:

  • Invest in resilient infrastructure where it’s needed most

  • Expand green jobs and economic opportunity equitably

  • Ensure universal access to clean air, clean water, and climate-related assistance

Like so many other social justice issues, progress cannot be achieved without centering, uplifting and meaningfully engaging historically marginalized communities in decision-making.

Environmental justice for all must be more than just aspirational. This requires policy, not platitudes.

TAKE ACTION:

Learn More & Support Organizations Leading the Charge

  • Environmental Defense Fund

  • Natural Resources Defense Council

  • California Environmental Justice Alliance

  • Greenaction for Health & Environmental Justice

  • Hawaii Alliance for Progressive Action

Your Voice Matters.

Right now, the Trump administration and Republican leaders are advancing policies that strip away environmental protections and abandon front line communities. We need leaders who will defend—not dismantle—our right to a healthy environment.

Tell them: Vote for clean air, clean water, and healthy communities.

Use this easy tool from Common Cause to call or email your representatives.

I am deeply concerned about the recent actions to weaken environmental protections and remove “Environmental Justice” from the EPA’s priorities. These moves sacrifice vulnerable communities and threaten public health, especially for low-income, Black, Brown, Indigenous, and rural families already burdened by environmental risks, underinvestment, and long-standing structural inequities.

I urge you to vote against any legislation that dismantles environmental safeguards and for policies that protect clean air, clean water, and the health of all communities. This is a matter of justice, health, safety, and human rights.

Environmental justice must be more than an aspiration—it must be a guarantee.

posts.title: TIME100 Philanthropy: Who the Spotlight Leaves Out
posts.author: mBOLDen Change
posts.excerpt: We’re kicking off our Substack the only way we know how: by challenging the dominant narrative.
posts.html:
Before we begin . . .

We’re kicking off our Substack the only way we know how: by challenging the dominant narrative.

This isn’t a welcome post or a mission statement — you can read who we are here.

What we’re sharing below is what this space is for: clear, unapologetic commentary on the systems shaping our world and the stories that keep them intact.

Philanthropy’s Power Problem

TIME magazine’s TIME100 Philanthropy list, celebrating the “100 most influential people shaping the future of giving at a pivotal moment,” reads like a society column. Perhaps that was the intent. But if so, let’s be honest about what’s being spotlighted: philanthropic celebrity.

To frame this group as the visionaries shaping the future of giving — without context, critique, or inclusion of grassroots perspectives — is to conflate visibility with vision, and power with progress.

The issue isn’t with who’s included — many of the individuals and institutions named are making real contributions. The problem is the premise: that billionaires, celebrities, and major foundation leaders are the ones shaping the future of giving. That idea doesn’t deserve celebration. It deserves scrutiny.

This framing reinforces a troubling power imbalance: one in which those who benefit most from inequality are also entrusted with solving it — where determining public priorities is a privilege reserved for those with private wealth or cultural capital. Where impact in philanthropy stems not from lived experience or proximity to harm, but from the ability to write a check or draw an audience.

Too often, philanthropy — especially in the hands of concentrated wealth — has become a form of privatized policy-making. It’s unelected power deciding which communities matter, which issues get traction, and which solutions are deemed worthy of investment. It is profoundly undemocratic — and instead of questioning that, the TIME100 list affirms and amplifies it.

We don’t need another echo chamber that elevates the already-elevated. We need a deeper, more honest conversation about who philanthropy is accountable to — and who is consistently left out of the frame. Because the truth is, change isn’t being engineered in boardrooms or ballrooms. It’s being built on the ground by organizers, mutual aid networks, community leaders, and everyday people doing the work with scarce resources and even less recognition.

Had TIME simply called this a list of top donors or philanthropic power players, that would have been more accurate. But to frame this group as the visionaries shaping the future of giving — without context, critique, or inclusion of grassroots perspectives — is to conflate visibility with vision, and power with progress.

At this pivotal moment, we don’t need philanthropy that mirrors social hierarchies or seeks legacy-building. We need a new model — one that listens more than it leads, follows the wisdom of those closest to the problems, and redistributes not just wealth but decision-making. The future of giving should be defined not by who has the most, but by who we choose to center.
